reviewerReport.lensLeakageCheck: Performed on all 39 English lines against the re-parsed Coptic (diplomatic text plus the Coptic Scriptorium normalisation and lemma layer). No English line carries a Wheel of Heaven reading. There is no 'Elohim', 'creators', 'planet', 'messenger' or capitalised 'Living One'. 'Sky' at 3, 9 and 20 is a context decision that cuts against a sky-located kingdom (3). 'Paradise' at 19 is the LXX term. No canonical-gospel wording was imported where the Coptic differs: 9 (no 'to sow', singular rock, worm), 20 (branch, not tree), 25 ('as your soul'), 27 (no 'Jesus said'), 31 ('village'), 35 ('binds his hands'), 36 (short form). The hard sayings keep the manuscript reading in the line: 7 ('the lion will become human' twice), 21 (negative robbers clause, a manuscript spelling paralleled at 22), 30 ('three gods … gods'), 37 ('without being ashamed'; '[then you will]' bracketed). Emendations and the Greek appear only in commentary. The lens appears in exactly three labelled paragraphs (3, 18, 19) pointing to the single speculative overlay entry.

The chapter `text` is byte-identical to source-cop-1.json for n=0–38. Conventions verified: [ ] at 8, 16, 22, 29 and 37 only; nomina sacra expanded silently; sky/heaven rule applied consistently; 'sons' only in the filial formulas (3, 28, 37), 'little child(ren)' for ϣⲏⲣⲉ ϣⲏⲙ (4, 21, 37).
reviewerReport.escalationReportAdjustments: Initial verdicts were formed before opening chapter-1-editor-report.md. After reading it, no per-unit verdict changed. The report added three things. (a) Its binding Blocks B/C list repeats "'will not taste death' (85, 111)", so the jitpe-mpmou revise now also asks for that list to be corrected (111 = 'will not see death'). (b) The 'sons' escalation looks ahead to Block B (logion 50), which exposed that the overlay's Greek-based criterion cannot decide sayings with no Greek; the shere-son-child revise now restates the criterion as the filial-formula pattern. (c) The text of the CENTRAL proposals: the lacuna-bracket extension was checked against the central rationale and found to conflict with its 'another witness' definition (revise: add an adoption sentence or keep the convention overlay-only); the other proposals and both deliberate non-extensions are approved.
reviewerReport.summary: 39 unit verdicts: 38 approve, 1 revise (THOM-3: the commentary should label Greek υἱοί as restored), 0 flag-for-human. 39 overlay entries: 35 approve, 3 revise (jitpe-mpmou: 111 is 'see death', not 'taste'; shere-son-child: Greek υἱοί claim overstated at 3 and 37, criterion restated for Blocks B/C; lion-and-man: Patterson–Meyer attribution appears wrong), 1 flag-for-human (the speculative WoH-reading entry, with a 'creating' → 'living' Father wording fix). Central proposals: add 'cop' approve; iēsous extension approve; kingdom-of-heaven → THOM-20 approve; lacuna-bracket extension revise (add Thomas adoption sentence or keep overlay-only); sower and beatitudes non-extensions approve. Escalated items: 7/30 manuscript readings approved; 'sons' approved (register question left open for the human); 33 'measure' approved; 21 unbracketed negative approved (supported by the same spelling at 22). Lens leakage: none in the English. Housekeeping (non-blocking): make the DeConick date consistent (2006 at THOM-0, 2007 at THOM-18 and two overlay entries). Translation quality is high: literal, unsmoothed, and faithful to the Coptic at every point checked. Status advanced to awaiting-human.

paragraphs.text: ⲛⲁⲉⲓ ⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ϣⲁϫⲉ ⲉⲑⲏⲡ⳿ ⲉⲛⲧⲁⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲉⲧⲟⲛϩ ϫⲟⲟⲩ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁϥⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ⲥⲟⲩ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲇⲓⲇⲩⲙⲟⲥ ⲓ̈ⲟⲩⲇⲁⲥ ⲑⲱⲙⲁⲥ

i18n.en: These are the hidden sayings that the living Jesus spoke, and Didymos Judas Thomas wrote them down.

notes.official:
**The hidden sayings.** ⲛ̄ϣⲁϫⲉ ⲉⲑⲏⲡ is literally 'the words that are hidden' (ϩⲏⲡ, stative of ϩⲱⲡ 'hide'). Lambdin's 'secret sayings' translates the Greek of P.Oxy. 654.1, οἱ λόγοι οἱ [ἀπόκρυφοι], where the adjective is a restoration. The WoH text follows the Coptic, and 'hidden' recurs at 5, 6 and 33.

ⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲉⲧⲟⲛϩ 'the living Jesus' is an ordinary relative clause ('Jesus who is alive'). Whether it means the risen Jesus or the one who has life is debated; the English keeps lower case, as at 3 ('the living Father') and 37 ('the living one').

**Didymos Judas Thomas.** Didymos (Greek) and Thomas (Aramaic *tᵓōmā*) both mean 'twin'; the triple name is the Syrian form of the apostle's name (Acts of Thomas; Book of Thomas, NHC II,7). The Greek incipit has, as restored, 'Judas who is also Thomas', without Didymos, and ἐλάλησεν 'spoke'.

**Date and setting.** The Coptic codex is fourth-century; the Greek fragments are third-century. The date of composition and Thomas's relation to the synoptic gospels are contested. Some scholars argue for an early collection of independent tradition that grew over time (Patterson 1993; DeConick 2005, 2006); others for a second-century text that knows the synoptics (Gathercole 2012, 2014; Goodacre 2012). How far Thomas belongs with later 'gnostic' literature is also debated. The apparatus records these positions without deciding between them.

paragraphs.text: ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ϫⲉⲡⲉⲧⲁϩⲉ ⲉⲑⲉⲣⲙⲏⲛⲉⲓⲁ ⲛⲛⲉⲉⲓϣⲁϫⲉ ϥⲛⲁϫⲓϯⲡⲉ ⲁⲛ ⲙ̄ⲡⲙⲟⲩ ·

i18n.en: And he said: Whoever finds the interpretation of these sayings will not taste death.

notes.official:
**Who speaks?** ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ 'And he said' has no named subject, and the Greek (P.Oxy. 654.3, καὶ εἶπεν) is equally open: the speaker may be Jesus or the compiler named in the incipit. The English keeps the ambiguity.

ϩⲉⲣⲙⲏⲛⲉⲓⲁ is the Greek loan ἑρμηνεία 'interpretation' (restored in the Greek). 'Will not taste death' keeps the Semitic idiom shared with Mt 16:28 and Jn 8:52 and is rendered the same way at 18 and 19. ⲡⲉⲧⲁϩⲉ is a Lycopolitan spelling of Sahidic ⲡⲉⲧⲛⲁϩⲉ (Dilley).

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲣⲉϥ⳿ⲗⲟ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲡⲉⲧ⳿ϣⲓⲛⲉ ⲉϥ⳿ϣⲓⲛⲉ ϣⲁⲛⲧⲉϥ⳿ϭⲓⲛⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ϩⲟⲧⲁⲛ⳿ ⲉϥϣⲁⲛϭⲓⲛⲉ ϥⲛⲁϣⲧⲣ̄ⲧⲣ̄ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲉϥϣⲁⲛϣⲧⲟⲣⲧⲣ̄ ϥⲛⲁⲣ̄ϣⲡⲏⲣⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ϥⲛⲁⲣ̄ⲣ̄ⲣ̄ⲟ ⲉϫⲙ̄ⲡⲧⲏⲣϥ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Let the one who seeks not cease seeking until he finds. And when he finds, he will be troubled; and when he is troubled, he will marvel, and he will reign over the All.

notes.official:
**Coptic and Greek diverge.** The Coptic sequence is seek, find, be troubled (ϣⲧⲟⲣⲧⲣ̄), marvel (ⲣ̄ϣⲡⲏⲣⲉ), reign over the All. The Greek of P.Oxy. 654.5-9 (partly restored) has no 'troubled' stage, reads 'he will be amazed' (θαμβηθήσεται) and 'having reigned he will rest' (ἀναπαήσεται), and has no 'over the All'. A related form, 'he who wonders will reign, and he who reigns will rest', is quoted by Clement of Alexandria (Strom. 2.9.45; 5.14.96). The WoH text follows the Coptic.

ⲡⲧⲏⲣϥ 'the All' is the set Nag Hammadi term for the totality; it is capitalised here and at 67 and 77. ⲣ̄ⲣⲣⲟ 'become king' is rendered 'reign'.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲉⲩϣⲁϫⲟⲟⲥ ⲛⲏⲧⲛ̄ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲛⲉⲧ⳿ⲥⲱⲕ ϩⲏⲧ⳿ⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄ ϫⲉⲉⲓⲥϩⲏⲏⲧⲉ ⲉⲧ⳿ⲙⲛⲧⲉⲣⲟ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲡⲉ ⲉⲉⲓⲉ ⲛ̄ϩⲁⲗⲏⲧ⳿ ⲛⲁ ⲣϣⲟⲣⲡ⳿ ⲉⲣⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲡⲉ ⲉⲩϣⲁⲛϫⲟⲟⲥ ⲛⲏⲧⲛ ϫⲉⲥϩⲛ̄ⲑⲁⲗⲁⲥⲥⲁ ⲉⲉⲓⲉ ⲛ̄ⲧⲃⲧ⳿ ⲛⲁ ⲣ̄ϣⲟⲣⲡ⳿ ⲉⲣⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲁⲗⲗⲁ ⲧⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ ⲥⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲛ̄ϩⲟⲩⲛ⳿ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲥⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲃⲁⲗ ϩⲟⲧⲁⲛ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲁⲛⲥⲟⲩⲱⲛⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄ ⲧⲟⲧⲉ ⲥⲉⲛⲁⲥⲟⲩⲱ⳯ⲧⲏⲛⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁⲉⲓⲙⲉ ϫⲉⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲡⲉ ⲛ̄ϣⲏⲣⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲓⲱⲧ ⲉⲧⲟⲛϩ ⲉϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲇⲉ ⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁⲥⲟⲩⲱⲛⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄ ⲁⲛ ⲉⲉⲓⲉ ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲟⲟⲡ⳿ ϩⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲙⲛ̄ⲧϩⲏⲕⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲡⲉ ⲧⲙⲛ̄ⲧϩⲏⲕⲉ

i18n.en: Jesus said: If those who lead you say to you, 'Behold, the kingdom is in the sky,' then the birds of the sky will go before you. If they say to you, 'It is in the sea,' then the fish will go before you. Rather, the kingdom is inside you, and it is outside you. When you come to know yourselves, then you will be known, and you will understand that it is you who are the sons of the living Father. But if you do not know yourselves, then you are in poverty, and it is you who are the poverty.

notes.official:
**'In the sky', not 'in heaven'.** Coptic ⲧⲡⲉ means both 'sky' and 'heaven'. The saying's joke depends on the same word in both clauses (if the kingdom is in the sky, the birds of the sky will get there first), so the English uses 'sky' twice, as Lambdin does. See `tpe-sky-heaven-context-rule-thomas-woh`.

**Greek differences** (P.Oxy. 654.9-21, much restored): the second location is 'under the earth', not 'in the sea'; 'the fish of the sea' enter ahead of you; the Greek adds 'whoever knows himself will find it' and lacks 'then you will be known'; the kingdom is usually restored as 'the kingdom [of God]'. Compare Lk 17:20-21. 'The sons of the living Father' agrees with the Greek of P.Oxy. 654 as usually restored (υἱοί; Attridge in Layton ed. 1989) (see `shere-son-child-thomas-woh`).

**Source note.** The diplomatic text reads ⲉⲩϣⲁϫⲟⲟⲥ, which the corpus normalises to the conditional ⲉⲩϣⲁⲛϫⲟⲟⲥ 'if they say'. The lemma aid records a supplied letter here that `text` does not mark. The English follows the normalised reading.

**Wheel of Heaven reading (interpretive; not part of the translation).** The saying denies that the kingdom is a place in the sky, so it gives no support to reading 'the kingdom' as a location among the stars. What a Wheel of Heaven reader may notice is the link it draws between self-knowledge and recognising oneself as a child of 'the living Father', which can be read alongside the canon's teaching that humans were made in the image of the Elohim. See `woh-reading-kingdom-within-beginning-end-five-trees-thomas-woh` (speculative).

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϥⲛⲁϫⲛⲁⲩ ⲁⲛ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲛ̄ϩⲗⲗⲟ ϩⲛ̄ⲛⲉϥϩⲟⲟⲩ ⲉϫⲛⲉⲟⲩⲕⲟⲩⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ϣⲏⲣⲉ ϣⲏⲙ ⲉϥϩⲛ̄ⲥⲁϣϥ̅ ⲛ̄ϩⲟⲟⲩ ⲉⲧⲃⲉⲡⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ ⲙ̄ⲡⲱⲛϩ ⲁⲩⲱ ϥⲛⲁⲱⲛϩ ϫⲉⲟⲩⲛϩⲁϩ ⲛϣⲟⲣⲡ ⲛⲁⲣ̄ϩⲁⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲛ̄ⲥⲉϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲟⲩⲁ ⲟⲩⲱⲧ

i18n.en: Jesus said: The man old in days will not hesitate to ask a little child of seven days about the place of life, and he will live. For many who are first will become last, and they will become a single one.

notes.official: The old man asks a child 'of seven days' about 'the place of life', a reversal of the usual order of authority; commentators often note that a seven-day-old boy has not yet reached the circumcision of the eighth day. The Greek (P.Oxy. 654.21-27) has the full proverb, 'many who are first will be last, and the last first'; the Coptic has only the first half, followed by 'and they will become a single one' (compare Mk 10:31). ⲟⲩⲁ ⲟⲩⲱⲧ 'a single one' is rendered the same way at 22 and 23.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲥⲟⲩⲱⲛⲡⲉⲧⲙ̄ⲡⲙ̄ⲧⲟ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲕϩⲟ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ⳿ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲉⲑⲏⲡ⳿ ⲉⲣⲟⲕ⳿ ϥⲛⲁϭⲱⲗⲡ⳿ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛⲁⲕ⳿ ⲙⲛ̄ⲗⲁⲁⲩ ⲅⲁⲣ ⲉϥϩⲏⲡ⳿ ⲉϥⲛⲁⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲁⲛ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Know what is in front of your face, and what is hidden from you will be revealed to you. For there is nothing hidden that will not be made manifest.

notes.official: The Coptic ends with 'there is nothing hidden that will not be made manifest' (compare Mk 4:22; Lk 8:17). The Greek (P.Oxy. 654.27-31) adds a further clause, 'and nothing buried that will not be raised', which the Coptic lacks. The WoH text follows the Coptic.

paragraphs.text: ⲁⲩϫⲛⲟⲩϥ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲛⲉϥ⳿ⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ⲡⲉϫⲁⲩ ⲛⲁϥ⳿ ϫⲉⲕ̂ⲟⲩⲱϣ ⲉⲧⲣⲛ̄︤ⲣ︥ⲛⲏⲥⲧⲉⲩⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲉϣ ⲧⲉ ⲑⲉ ⲉⲛⲁϣⲗⲏⲗ ⲉⲛⲁϯⲉⲗⲉⲏⲙⲟⲥⲩⲛⲏ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲉⲛⲁⲣⲡⲁⲣⲁⲧⲏⲣⲉⲓ ⲉⲟⲩ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲟⲩⲱⲙ⳿ ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲙ̄ⲡⲣ̄ϫⲉϭⲟⲗ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲧⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲥⲧⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟϥ⳿ ⲙ̄ⲡⲣ̄ⲁⲁϥ ϫⲉⲥⲉϭⲟⲗⲡ⳿ ⲧⲏⲣⲟⲩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲙⲧⲟ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛ̄ⲧⲡⲉ ⲙⲛ̄ⲗⲁⲁⲩ ⲅⲁⲣ ⲉϥϩⲏⲡ · ⲉϥⲛⲁⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲁⲛ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲙⲛⲗⲁⲁⲩ ⲉϥϩⲟⲃ︤ⲥ︥ ⲉⲩⲛⲁϭⲱ ⲟⲩⲉϣⲛ̄ ϭⲟⲗⲡϥ⳿

i18n.en: His disciples questioned him; they said to him: Do you want us to fast? And in what way shall we pray? Shall we give alms? And what shall we observe with regard to eating? Jesus said: Do not lie, and what you hate, do not do. For all things are revealed in the sight of heaven. For there is nothing hidden that will not be made manifest, and there is nothing covered that will remain without being uncovered.

notes.official:
**Coptic and Greek differ in the question and the reason.** In the Greek (P.Oxy. 654.32-40) the disciples ask 'How shall we fast?'; the Coptic has ⲕⲟⲩⲱϣ ⲉⲧⲣⲛ̄ⲣ̄ⲛⲏⲥⲧⲉⲩⲉ 'Do you want us to fast?'. The Greek grounds the answer in 'all things are disclosed before the truth' (ἐνώπιον τῆς ἀληθείας, partly restored); the Coptic has ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲙⲧⲟ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛ̄ⲧⲡⲉ 'in the sight of heaven'. ⲧⲡⲉ is 'heaven' here, not 'sky', because the sense is the divine vantage point.

The questions about fasting, prayer and alms are answered directly only at logion 14. Dilley notes an unusual circumstantial after a definite antecedent in this saying.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲟⲩⲙⲁⲕⲁⲣⲓⲟⲥ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲙⲟⲩⲉⲓ ⲡⲁⲉⲓ ⲉⲧⲉⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲛⲁⲟⲩⲟⲙϥ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲡⲙⲟⲩⲉⲓ ϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ϥⲃⲏⲧ · ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲡⲁⲉⲓ ⲉⲧⲉⲡⲙⲟⲩⲉⲓ ⲛⲁⲟⲩⲟⲙϥ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲙⲟⲩⲉⲓ ⲛⲁϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Blessed is the lion that the man will eat, and the lion will become human. And loathsome is the man whom the lion will eat, and the lion will become human.

notes.official:
**The textual crux.** The manuscript ends ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲙⲟⲩⲉⲓ ⲛⲁϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ 'and the lion will become human', repeating the outcome of the first half. Many editors and translators emend to 'and the man will become lion', which gives the symmetrical antithesis the saying seems to need. Others defend the transmitted text as meaningful (Jackson 1985 reads it against Platonic and gnostic lion imagery for the passions). No Greek survives beyond traces (P.Oxy. 654.40-42). The WoH text prints the manuscript reading; the emendation is a conjecture.

ϥⲃⲏⲧ, the stative of ⲃⲱⲧⲉ 'be abhorrent', is rendered 'loathsome' (Lambdin: 'cursed'). 'Blessed is' renders the singular ⲟⲩⲙⲁⲕⲁⲣⲓⲟⲥ ⲡⲉ; the saying has no synoptic parallel.

paragraphs.text: ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ϫⲉⲉⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲧⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲛ ⲁⲩⲟⲩⲱϩⲉ ⲣ̄ⲣⲙⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧ⳿ ⲡⲁⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁϩⲛⲟⲩϫⲉ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉϥⲁⲃⲱ ⲉⲑⲁⲗⲁⲥⲥⲁ ⲁϥⲥⲱⲕ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲥ ⲉϩⲣⲁⲓ̈ ϩⲛ̄ⲑⲁⲗⲁⲥⲥⲁ ⲉⲥⲙⲉϩ ⲛⲧⲃⲧ ⲛ̄ⲕⲟⲩⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ ϩⲣⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧⲟⲩ ⲁϥϩⲉ ⲁⲩⲛⲟϭ ⲛ̄ⲧⲃ︤ⲧ︥ ⲉⲛⲁⲛⲟⲩϥ⳿ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲡⲟⲩⲱϩⲉ ⲣ̄ⲣⲙⲛϩⲏⲧ̂ ⲁϥⲛⲟⲩϫⲉ ⲛ̄ⲛ̄ⲕⲟⲩⲉⲓ ⲧⲏⲣⲟⲩ ⲛⲧⲃⲧ⳿ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲉ[ⲡⲉ]ⲥⲏⲧ̂ ⲉⲑⲁⲗⲁⲥⲥⲁ ⲁϥⲥⲱⲧⲡ · ⲙ̄ⲡⲛⲟϭ ⲛ̄ⲧⲃ︤ⲧ︥ ⲭⲱⲣⲓⲥϩⲓⲥⲉ ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲟⲩⲛⲙⲁⲁϫⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟϥ ⲉⲥⲱⲧⲙ̄ ⲙⲁⲣⲉϥ̂ⲥⲱⲧⲙ

i18n.en: And he said: The man is like a wise fisherman who cast his net into the sea; he drew it up from the sea full of small fish. Among them the wise fisherman found a fine large fish. He threw all the small fish out, [down] into the sea; he chose the large fish without difficulty. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.

notes.official:
**Restoration.** ⲉ[ⲡⲉ]ⲥⲏⲧ 'down' stands on restored letters and is bracketed: '[down] into the sea' (see `restored-text-bracket-and-sigla-convention-thomas-woh`). The lemma aid counts two supplied spans here against one bracket in `text`. The corpus also normalises ⲁⲩⲟⲩⲱϩⲉ and ⲁⲩⲛⲟϭ to circumstantial ⲉⲩ-, which the English follows ('a wise fisherman', 'a fine large fish').

Here 'the man' (ⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ) is the subject of the comparison. In Matthew's dragnet parable (Mt 13:47-48) the kingdom is compared and the catch is sorted into good and bad; in Thomas one large fish is chosen and all the small ones are thrown back.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲉⲓⲥϩⲏⲏⲧⲉ · ⲁϥⲉⲓ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲡⲉⲧ⳿ⲥⲓⲧⲉ ⲁϥⲙⲉϩⲧⲟⲟⲧϥ︦ ⲁϥⲛⲟⲩϫⲉ ⲁϩⲟⲉⲓⲛⲉ ⲙⲉⲛ ϩⲉ ⲉϫⲛⲧⲉϩⲓⲏ⳿ ⲁⲩⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲛ̄ϩⲁⲗⲁⲧⲉ ⲁⲩⲕⲁⲧϥⲟⲩ ϩⲛ̄ⲕⲟⲟⲩⲉ ⲁⲩϩⲉ ⲉϫⲛ̄ⲧⲡⲉⲧⲣⲁ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲙ̄ⲡⲟⲩϫⲉⲛⲟⲩⲛⲉ ⲉⲡⲉⲥⲏⲧ̂ ⲉⲡⲕⲁϩ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲙ̄ⲡⲟⲩⲧⲉⲩⲉϩⲙ︤ⲥ︥ ⲉϩⲣⲁⲓ̈ ⲉⲧⲡⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ϩⲛ̄ⲕⲟⲟⲩⲉ ⲁⲩϩⲉ ⲉϫⲛ̄ⲛ̄ϣⲟ(ⲛ)ⲧⲉ ⲁⲩⲱϭⲧ⳿ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉϭⲣⲟϭ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁⲡϥⲛ︤ⲧ︥ ⲟⲩⲟⲙⲟⲩ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁϩⲛ̄ⲕⲟⲟⲩⲉ ϩⲉ ⲉϫⲛ̄ⲡⲕⲁϩ ⲉⲧⲛⲁⲛⲟⲩϥ⳿ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁϥϯⲕⲁⲣⲡⲟⲥ ⲉϩⲣⲁⲓ̈ ⲉⲧⲡⲉ ⲉⲛⲁⲛⲟⲩϥ⳿ ⲁϥⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ⲥⲉ ⲉⲥⲟⲧⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ϣⲉϫⲟⲩⲱⲧ⳿ ⲉⲥⲟⲧⲉ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Behold, the sower went out; he filled his hand and cast. Some fell on the path; the birds came and gathered them up. Others fell on the rock, and they did not send root down into the soil, and they did not send up ears toward the sky. And others fell on the thorns; they choked the seed, and the worm ate them. And others fell on the good soil, and it produced good fruit up toward the sky; it bore sixty per measure and one hundred twenty per measure.

notes.official:
**Thomas's sower.** The opening matches matthew-woh ('Behold, the sower went out'), but the details are Thomas's own: no 'to sow', a single 'rock', ears that do not rise 'toward the sky', a worm that eats the choked seed, and yields of 'sixty per measure and one hundred twenty per measure' (ⲉⲥⲟⲧⲉ). There is no allegorical interpretation (contrast Mt 13:18-23). The central Matthean sower entry is not applied; see `sower-parable-coptic-form-and-eisheete-behold-thomas-woh`.

ⲛ̄ϣⲟ(ⲛ)ⲧⲉ 'the thorns' contains an editorially supplied ⲛ, rendered silently.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲁⲉⲓⲛⲟⲩϫⲉ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲕⲱϩⲧ⳿ ⲉϫⲛ̄ⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲉⲓⲥϩⲏⲏⲧⲉ ϯⲁⲣⲉϩ ⲉⲣⲟϥ⳿ ϣⲁⲛⲧⲉϥϫⲉⲣⲟ

i18n.en: Jesus said: I have cast fire upon the world, and behold, I am guarding it until it blazes.

notes.official:
Compare Lk 12:49 ('I came to cast fire upon the earth').

**Source note.** The diplomatic ϯⲁⲣⲉϩ is normalised by the corpus to ϯϩⲁⲣⲉϩ 'I guard'. The lemma aid records a supplied letter that `text` does not mark. The English follows the normalised reading.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲧⲉⲉⲓⲡⲉ ⲛⲁⲣ̄ⲡⲁⲣⲁⲅⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲧⲡⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲥ ⲛⲁⲣ̄ⲡⲁⲣⲁⲅⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲛⲉⲧⲙⲟⲟⲩⲧ ⲥⲉⲟⲛϩ ⲁⲛ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲛⲉⲧⲟⲛϩ ⲥⲉⲛⲁⲙⲟⲩ ⲁⲛ ⲛ̄ϩⲟⲟⲩ ⲛⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲱⲙ⳿ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲙⲟⲟⲩⲧ⳿ ⲛⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲉⲓⲣⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟϥ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲟⲛϩ ϩⲟⲧⲁⲛ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲁⲛϣⲱⲡⲉ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ ⲟⲩ ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁⲁϥ ϩⲙ̄ⲫⲟⲟⲩ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲟ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲁ ⲁⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲉⲓⲣⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲥⲛⲁⲩ ϩⲟⲧⲁⲛ ⲇⲉ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲁϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲛ̄ⲥⲛⲁⲩ · ⲟⲩ ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲛⲁⲁϥ ·

i18n.en: Jesus said: This heaven will pass away, and the one above it will pass away. And the dead are not alive, and the living will not die. In the days when you ate what is dead, you made it what is alive. When you come to be in the light, what will you do? On the day when you were one, you became two. But when you become two, what will you do?

notes.official:
**Two heavens.** 'This heaven will pass away, and the one above it will pass away' presupposes layered heavens, so ⲧⲡⲉ is 'heaven' here, not 'sky'. Compare Mk 13:31.

The past forms are kept literal: 'In the days when you ate what is dead, you made it what is alive'. 'On the day when you were one, you became two' uses plain ⲟⲩⲁ 'one', the theme of 4, 22 and 23. Dilley notes an elision in this saying.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ⲛ̄ⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲥⲟⲟⲩⲛ ϫⲉⲕⲛⲁⲃⲱⲕ ⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲟⲧ︤ⲛ︥ ⲛⲓⲙ⳿ ⲡⲉ ⲉⲧⲛⲁⲣ̄ⲛⲟϭ ⲉϩⲣⲁⲓ̈ ⲉϫⲱⲛ ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲛⲁⲩ ϫⲉⲡⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲉⲓ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁⲃⲱⲕ̂ ϣⲁⲓ̈ⲁⲕⲱⲃⲟⲥ ⲡⲇⲓⲕⲁⲓⲟⲥ ⲡⲁⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲧⲡⲉ ⲙⲛ̄ⲡⲕⲁϩ ϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲉⲧⲃⲏⲧϥ̅

i18n.en: The disciples said to Jesus: We know that you will depart from us. Who is it that will be great over us? Jesus said to them: Wherever you have come to, you are to go to James the Righteous, for whose sake heaven and earth came into being.

notes.official:
**James the Righteous.** ⲓ̈ⲁⲕⲱⲃⲟⲥ ⲡⲇⲓⲕⲁⲓⲟⲥ is the James whom later tradition calls 'the Just' (Hegesippus in Eusebius, Hist. eccl. 2.23): the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem community (Gal 1:19; 2:9). 'Righteous' renders ⲇⲓⲕⲁⲓⲟⲥ as at 13 ('a righteous angel').

ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁⲃⲱⲕ is the focalising (second) future. It puts the stress on 'to James' and, in answer to 'who will lead us?', has directive force, hence 'you are to go' (Lambdin). ⲡⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲉⲓ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ is 'the place you have come to'. 'For whose sake heaven and earth came into being' uses an idiom found in Jewish texts that say the world was created for the sake of the righteous or of Israel (e.g. 4 Ezra 6:55).

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉϥⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ϫⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲛⲧ⳿ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϫⲟⲟⲥ ⲛⲁⲉⲓ ϫⲉⲉⲉ⟨ⲓ⟩ⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ⲛⲓⲙ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁϥ⳿ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲥⲓⲙⲱⲛ ⲡⲉⲧⲣⲟⲥ ϫⲉⲉⲕⲉⲓⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲁⲅ⳿ⲅⲉⲗⲟⲥ ⲛ̄ⲇⲓⲕⲁⲓⲟⲥ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁϥ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲙⲁⲑ⳿ⲑⲁⲓⲟⲥ ϫⲉⲉⲕⲉⲓⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲙ̄ⲫⲓⲗⲟⲥⲟⲫⲟⲥ ⲛ̄ⲣⲛ̄ⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧ⳿ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁϥ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲑⲱⲙⲁⲥ ϫⲉⲡⲥⲁϩ ϩⲟⲗⲱⲥ ⲧⲁⲧⲁⲡⲣⲟ ⲛⲁϣ⟨ϣ⟩ⲁⲡϥ⳿ ⲁⲛ ⲉⲧⲣⲁϫⲟⲟⲥ ϫⲉⲉⲕⲉⲓⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ⲛⲓⲙ⳿ ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓⲏ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲁⲛⲟⲕ⳿ ⲡⲉⲕ⳿ⲥⲁϩ ⲁⲛ ⲉⲡⲉⲓⲁⲕⲥⲱ ⲁⲕϯϩⲉ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲡⲏⲅⲏ ⲉⲧⲃⲣ̄ⲃⲣⲉⲧⲁⲉⲓ ⲧⲁⲉⲓ ⲁⲛⲟⲕ⳿ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲉⲓϣⲓⲧⲥ︥ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁϥϫⲓⲧϥ̅ ⲁϥⲁⲛⲁⲭⲱⲣⲉⲓ ⲁϥϫⲱ ⲛⲁϥ ⲛ̄ϣⲟⲙⲧ̂ ⲛ̄ϣⲁϫⲉ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲣⲉⲑⲱⲙⲁⲥ ⲇⲉ ⲉⲓ ϣⲁⲛⲉϥ⳿ϣⲃⲉⲉⲣ⳿ ⲁⲩϫⲛⲟⲩϥ⳿ ϫⲉⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲟⲟⲥ ϫⲉⲟⲩ ⲛⲁⲕ⳿ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ̂ ⲛⲁⲩ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲑⲱⲙⲁⲥ ϫⲉⲉⲓϣⲁⲛ̂ϫⲱ ⲛⲏⲧⲛ̄ ⲟⲩⲁ ϩⲛ̄ⲛ̄ⲛϣⲁϫⲉ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁϥϫⲟⲟⲩ ⲛⲁⲉⲓ ⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁϥⲓⲱⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲛⲟⲩϫⲉ ⲉⲣⲟⲉⲓ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲟⲩⲕⲱϩⲧ⳿ ⲉⲓ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ⲛ̄ⲱⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ⲥⲣⲱϩⲕ⳿ ⲙ̄ⲙⲱⲧⲛ̄

i18n.en: Jesus said to his disciples: Compare me, and tell me whom I am like. Simon Peter said to him: You are like a righteous angel. Matthew said to him: You are like a wise philosopher. Thomas said to him: Teacher, my mouth is wholly unable to say whom you are like. Jesus said: I am not your teacher, for you have drunk, you have become drunk from the bubbling spring that I have measured out. And he took him, withdrew, and spoke three words to him. Now when Thomas came to his companions, they asked him: What did Jesus say to you? Thomas said to them: If I tell you one of the words that he spoke to me, you will pick up stones and throw them at me, and a fire will come out of the stones and burn you up.

notes.official:
**Who is Jesus like?** The scene parallels Mk 8:27-30, but here Peter and Matthew give inadequate answers and Thomas says he cannot answer at all. 'Teacher' renders ⲡⲥⲁϩ both in Thomas's address and in Jesus's reply ('I am not your teacher'), which is the point of the exchange. ⲁⲅⲅⲉⲗⲟⲥ is rendered 'angel', although the Greek loan can also mean 'messenger'. 'The bubbling spring that I have measured out' renders ϣⲓ 'measure' literally (Lambdin); some translations paraphrase 'tended'. The 'three words' are not disclosed.

**Sigla.** ⲉⲉ⟨ⲓ⟩ⲛⲉ and ⲛⲁϣ⟨ϣ⟩ⲁⲡϥ contain letters supplied by the editor, and Dilley notes a metathesis. They are rendered silently.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲛⲁⲩ ϫⲉⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲁⲛⲣ̄ⲛⲏⲥⲧⲉⲩⲉ ⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁϫⲡⲟ ⲛⲏⲧⲛ̄ ⲛ̄ⲛⲟⲩⲛⲟⲃⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲁ(ⲛ)ϣⲗⲏⲗ⳿ ⲥⲉⲛⲁⲣ̄ⲕⲁⲧⲁⲕⲣⲓⲛⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲁⲛϯⲉⲗⲉⲏⲙⲟⲥⲩⲛⲏ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁⲉⲓⲣⲉ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲕⲁⲕⲟⲛ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲧⲙⲡ︤ⲛ︥︤ⲁ︥ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲁⲛⲃⲱⲕ⳿ ⲉϩⲟⲩⲛ ⲉⲕⲁϩ ⲛⲓⲙ ⲁⲩⲱ 'ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲟϣⲉ ϩⲛ̄ⲛ̄ⲭⲱⲣⲁ ⲉⲩϣⲁⲣ̄ⲡⲁⲣⲁⲇⲉⲭⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲡⲉⲧⲟⲩⲛⲁⲕⲁⲁϥ ϩⲁⲣⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲟⲩⲟⲙϥ̅ ⲛⲉⲧϣⲱⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧⲟⲩ ⲉⲣⲓⲑⲉⲣⲁⲡⲉⲩⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲟⲩ ⲡⲉⲧⲛⲁⲃⲱⲕ ⲅⲁⲣ⳿ ⲉϩⲟⲩⲛ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲡⲣⲟ ϥⲛⲁϫⲱϩⲙ̄ⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄ ⲁⲛ⳿ ⲁⲗⲗⲁ ⲡⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲛⲏⲩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ⳿ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲡⲣⲟ ⲛ̄ⲧⲟϥ ⲡⲉⲧⲛⲁϫⲁϩⲙ̄ⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ

i18n.en: Jesus said to them: If you fast, you will beget a sin for yourselves; and if you pray, you will be condemned; and if you give alms, you will do harm to your spirits. And if you go into any land and walk about in the regions, if they receive you, eat what they set before you; heal the sick among them. For what goes into your mouth will not defile you; rather, what comes out of your mouth, it is that which will defile you.

notes.official:
**The answer to logion 6.** This saying answers the questions of 6 (fasting, prayer, alms) with a reversal: each practice is said to do harm. The second half parallels Lk 10:8-9 (eat what is set before you; heal the sick) and Mk 7:15 / Mt 15:11 (what goes in does not defile). 'Your spirits' renders the plural ⲛⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲡⲛ︤ⲁ︥, the human spirit, hence lower case.

**Source notes.** ϣⲁ(ⲛ) contains an editorially supplied ⲛ, rendered silently. The diplomatic text has a stray ASCII apostrophe before ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲟϣⲉ, apparently an encoding artefact rather than a manuscript feature. The source file is not altered, and the English is unaffected.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉϩⲟⲧⲁⲛ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲁⲛⲛⲁⲩ ⲉⲡⲉⲧⲉⲙ̄ⲡⲟⲩϫⲡⲟϥ⳿ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲥϩⲓⲙⲉ ⲡⲉϩⲧ⳿ⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄ ⲉϫⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲛ̄ϩⲟ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲱϣⲧ ⲛⲁϥ̂ ⲡⲉⲧⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲉⲓⲱⲧ⳿

i18n.en: Jesus said: When you see one who was not born of woman, prostrate yourselves on your faces and worship him; that one is your Father.

notes.official: ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲙ̄ⲡⲟⲩϫⲡⲟϥ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲥϩⲓⲙⲉ is literally 'the one whom they did not beget from the woman'. 'Born of woman' follows the English idiom of Job 14:1 and Mt 11:11. 'Your Father' is capitalised as the divine referent (see `eiot-father-capitalisation-thomas-woh`).

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲧⲁⲭⲁ ⲉⲩⲙⲉⲉⲩⲉ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ ϫⲉⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲉⲓⲉⲓ ⲉⲛⲟⲩϫⲉ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲉⲓⲣⲏⲛⲏ ⲉϫⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲥⲉⲥⲟⲟⲩⲛ ⲁⲛ ϫⲉⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲉⲓⲉⲓ ⲁⲛⲟⲩϫⲉ ⲛ̄ϩⲛ̄ⲡⲱⲣϫ⳿ ⲉϫⲛ̄ⲡⲕⲁϩ ⲟⲩⲕⲱϩⲧ ⲟⲩⲥⲏϥⲉ⳿ ⲟⲩⲡⲟⲗⲉⲙⲟⲥ ⲟⲩⲛ̄ϯⲟⲩ ⲅⲁⲣ ⲛⲁϣⲱ[ⲡⲉ] ϩⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲏⲉⲓ ⲟⲩⲛ̄ϣⲟⲙⲧ ⲛⲁϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲉϫⲛ̄ⲥⲛⲁⲩ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲥⲛⲁⲩ ⲉϫⲛ̄ϣⲟⲙⲧ⳿ ⲡⲉⲓⲱⲧ⳿ ⲉϫⲙ̄ⲡϣⲏⲣⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡϣⲏⲣⲉ ⲉϫⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲓⲱⲧ⳿ ⲁⲩⲱ · ⲥⲉⲛⲁⲱϩⲉ ⲉⲣⲁⲧⲟⲩ ⲉⲩⲟ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲛⲁⲭⲟⲥ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Perhaps people think that I have come to cast peace upon the world, and they do not know that I have come to cast divisions upon the earth: fire, sword, war. For there will [be] five in a house: three will be against two and two against three, the father against the son and the son against the father. And they will stand as solitary ones.

notes.official:
**Solitary ones.** ⲉⲩⲟ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲛⲁⲭⲟⲥ uses the Greek loan μοναχός 'single, solitary', which later became the standard word for 'monk'. It is rendered 'solitary ones' without choosing between the readings in the commentaries: unmarried; undivided or unified; or separated from family, which fits the household strife of this saying. It is kept distinct from ⲟⲩⲁ ⲟⲩⲱⲧ 'a single one' (4, 22, 23). The word recurs at 49 and 75.

Compare Lk 12:49-53 and Mt 10:34-36. Thomas adds 'fire' to sword and war; the five-in-a-house arithmetic matches Luke. 'There will [be] five' brackets 'be' because ⲛⲁϣⲱ[ⲡⲉ] is partly restored.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉϯⲛⲁϯ ⲛⲏⲧⲛ̄ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲃⲁⲗ ⲛⲁⲩ ⲉⲣⲟϥ⳿ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲙⲁⲁϫⲉ ⲥⲟⲧⲙⲉϥ⳿ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲙⲡⲉϭⲓϫ⳿ ϭⲙ̄ϭⲱⲙϥ̅ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉϥⲉⲓ ⲉϩⲣⲁⲓ̈ ϩⲓⲫⲏⲧ⳿ ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ

i18n.en: Jesus said: I will give you what eye has not seen, and what ear has not heard, and what hand has not touched, and what has not come up into the heart of man.

notes.official: Compare 1 Cor 2:9 ('what no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man conceived'), a saying widely quoted in early Jewish and Christian texts. Thomas adds 'what hand has not touched'.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ⲛ̄ⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉϫⲟⲟⲥ ⲉⲣⲟⲛ ϫⲉⲧⲛ̄ϩⲁⲏ ⲉⲥⲛⲁϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲛ̄ⲁϣ ⲛ̄ϩⲉ ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲁⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϭⲱⲗⲡ⳿ ⲅⲁⲣ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲣⲭⲏ ϫⲉⲕⲁⲁⲥ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁϣⲓⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁⲑⲁϩⲏ ϫⲉϩⲙ̄ⲡⲙⲁ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲁⲣⲭⲏ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ ⲉⲑⲁϩⲏ ⲛⲁϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ ⲟⲩⲙⲁⲕⲁⲣⲓⲟⲥ ⲡⲉⲧⲛⲁϩⲱϩⲉ ⲉⲣⲁⲧϥ̄ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲣⲭⲏ ⲁⲩⲱ ϥⲛⲁⲥⲟⲩⲱⲛⲑϩⲁⲏ ⲁⲩⲱ ϥⲛⲁϫⲓϯⲡⲉ ⲁⲛ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲩ

i18n.en: The disciples said to Jesus: Tell us how our end will come about. Jesus said: Have you then uncovered the beginning, that you seek the end? For where the beginning is, there the end will be. Blessed is the one who will stand at the beginning: he will know the end, and he will not taste death.

notes.official:
**Beginning and end.** ⲧⲁⲣⲭⲏ (Greek loan) and ⲑⲁϩⲏ (native ϩⲁⲏ) are rendered 'the beginning' and 'the end'. The saying answers a question about the end by pointing back to the beginning, a theme commentators connect with Thomas's interest in the primordial state (DeConick 2006; Gathercole 2014).

**Source note.** In ⲥⲟⲩⲱⲛⲑϩⲁⲏ the scribe wrote and erased a ϩ (rasura, Dilley); the lemma aid records a supplied element that `text` does not mark. 'He will know the end' is unaffected. The disciples' 'our end' follows the corpus normalisation ⲧⲉⲛϩⲁⲏ.

**Wheel of Heaven reading (interpretive; not part of the translation).** A Wheel of Heaven reader will hear in 'where the beginning is, there the end will be' an echo of the cyclical framework of precessional ages from which the project takes its name. The saying itself speaks of individual knowledge and of not tasting death, not of cosmic cycles. See `woh-reading-kingdom-within-beginning-end-five-trees-thomas-woh` (speculative).

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲟⲩⲙⲁⲕⲁⲣⲓⲟⲥ ⲡⲉⲛⲧⲁϩϣⲱⲡⲉ ϩⲁⲧⲉϩⲏ ⲉⲙⲡⲁⲧⲉϥϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲁⲛϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲛⲁⲉⲓ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲥⲱⲧⲙ̄ ⲁⲛⲁϣⲁϫⲉ ⲛⲉⲉⲓⲱⲛⲉ ⲛⲁⲣ̄ⲇⲓⲁⲕⲟⲛⲉⲓ ⲛⲏⲧⲛ̄ ⲟⲩⲛ̄ⲧⲏⲧⲛ̄ ⲅⲁⲣ̂ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ ⲛ̄ϯⲟⲩ ⲛ̄ϣⲏⲛ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲁⲣⲁⲇⲓⲥⲟⲥ ⲉⲥⲉⲕⲓⲙ ⲁⲛ ⲛ̄ϣⲱⲙ⳿ ⲙ̄ⲡⲣⲱ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲙⲁⲣⲉⲛⲟⲩϭⲱⲃⲉ ϩⲉ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲡⲉⲧ⳿ⲛⲁⲥⲟⲩⲱⲛⲟⲩ ϥⲛⲁϫⲓϯⲡⲉ ⲁⲛ⳿ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲩ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Blessed is the one who came into being before he came into being. If you become disciples to me and listen to my sayings, these stones will serve you. For you have five trees in Paradise that do not move in summer or in winter, and their leaves do not fall. Whoever knows them will not taste death.

notes.official:
**Five trees in Paradise.** ⲡⲁⲣⲁⲇⲓⲥⲟⲥ is the Septuagint word for the garden of Eden (Gen 2:8). Genesis names two trees; Thomas's five unchanging trees have no biblical source. Five trees recur in later Coptic literature, including Manichaean texts, where they are read allegorically. 'That do not move in summer or in winter' renders ⲉⲥⲉⲕⲓⲙ ⲁⲛ ⲛ̄ϣⲱⲙ ⲙ̄ⲡⲣⲱ literally (Lambdin: 'remain undisturbed summer and winter').

'Blessed is the one who came into being before he came into being' is a paradox of pre-existence. 'Blessed is' renders the singular ⲟⲩⲙⲁⲕⲁⲣⲓⲟⲥ ⲡⲉ, as at 7 and 18.

**Wheel of Heaven reading (interpretive; not part of the translation).** The canon reads the Eden of Genesis 2 as the place where the Elohim worked, and a Wheel of Heaven reader may set Thomas's five unchanging trees beside that reading. Thomas says nothing about the trees beyond their permanence, and the canon does not cite this saying. See `woh-reading-kingdom-within-beginning-end-five-trees-thomas-woh` (speculative).

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ⲛ̄ⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉϫⲟⲟⲥ ⲉⲣⲟⲛ ϫⲉⲧⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ ⲛⲙ̄ⲡⲏⲩⲉ ⲉⲥⲧⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲛ ⲉⲛⲓⲙ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁⲩ ϫⲉⲉⲥⲧⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲛ ⲁⲩⲃⲗ︦ⲃⲓⲗⲉ ⲛ̄ϣⲗ︦ⲧⲁⲙ ⟨ⲥ⟩ⲥⲟⲃ︤ⲕ︥ ⲡⲁⲣⲁⲛ̄ϭⲣⲟϭ ⲧⲏⲣⲟⲩ ϩⲟⲧⲁⲛ ⲇⲉ ⲉⲥϣⲁ(ⲛ)ϩⲉ ⲉϫⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲁϩ ⲉⲧⲟⲩⲣ̄ϩⲱⲃ ⲉⲣⲟϥ ϣⲁϥⲧⲉⲩⲟ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛ̄ⲛⲟⲩⲛⲟϭ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲣ ⲛ̄ϥϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲛ̄ⲥⲕⲉⲡⲏ ⲛ̄ϩⲁⲗⲁⲧⲉ ⲛ̄ⲧⲡⲉ

i18n.en: The disciples said to Jesus: Tell us what the kingdom of the heavens is like. He said to them: It is like a mustard seed. It is smaller than all seeds; but when it falls on the soil that is tilled, it sends forth a great branch and becomes a shelter for the birds of the sky.

notes.official:
'The kingdom of the heavens' keeps the Coptic plural ⲙ̄ⲡⲏⲩⲉ, as matthew-woh does for Greek τῶν οὐρανῶν. Thomas also uses the phrase at 54 and 114, so it is not exclusively Matthean (central `kingdom-of-heaven-basileia-tōn-ouranōn-mt-distinctive-cross-corpus-hebrew-malkhut-shamayim`). 'The birds of the sky' follows the ⲧⲡⲉ context rule and matthew-woh 13:32.

Compare Mk 4:30-32 (a plant with large branches, as here) and Mt 13:31-32 / Lk 13:18-19 (a tree). Thomas adds that the soil is 'tilled'.

**Sigla.** ⟨ⲥ⟩ⲥⲟⲃ︤ⲕ︥ and ϣⲁ(ⲛ) contain editorially supplied letters, rendered silently.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲙⲁⲣⲓϩⲁⲙ ⲛ̄ⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲉⲛⲉⲕⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ⲉⲓⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ⲛⲓⲙ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ⳿ ϫⲉⲉⲩⲉⲓⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ϩⲛ̄ϣⲏⲣⲉ ϣⲏⲙ⳿ ⲉⲩϭⲉⲗⲓⲧ⳿ ⲁⲩⲥⲱϣⲉ ⲉⲧⲱⲟⲩ ⲁⲛ ⲧⲉ ϩⲟⲧⲁⲛ ⲉⲩϣⲁⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲛ̄ϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ ⲛ̄ⲧⲥⲱϣⲉ ⲥⲉⲛⲁϫⲟⲟⲥ ϫⲉⲕⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲥⲱϣⲉ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛⲁⲛ ⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲟⲩ ⲥⲉⲕⲁⲕⲁϩⲏⲩ ⲙ̄ⲡⲟⲩⲙ̄ⲧⲟ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲉⲧⲣⲟⲩⲕⲁⲁⲥ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛⲁⲩ ⲛ̄ⲥⲉϯⲧⲟⲩⲥⲱϣⲉ ⲛⲁⲩ ⲇⲓⲁⲧⲟⲩⲧⲟ ϯϫⲱ ⲙⲙⲟⲥ ϫⲉⲉϥ⳿ϣⲁⲉⲓⲙⲉ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲡϫⲉⲥϩⲛ̄ⲏⲉⲓ ϫⲉϥⲛⲏⲩ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲡⲣⲉϥϫⲓⲟⲩⲉ ϥⲛⲁⲣⲟⲉⲓⲥ ⲉⲙⲡⲁⲧⲉϥ⳿ⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ϥⲧⲙⲕⲁⲁϥ̂ ⲉϣⲟϫⲧ⳿ ⲉϩⲟⲩⲛ ⲉⲡⲉϥⲏⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲉϥ⳿ⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ ⲉⲧⲣⲉϥϥⲓ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉϥ̂ⲥⲕⲉⲩⲟⲥ ⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲇⲉ ⲣⲟⲉⲓⲥ ϩⲁⲧⲉϩⲏ ⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ ⲙⲟⲩⲣ⳿ ⲙ̄ⲙⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲉϫⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲧⲛ̄ϯⲡⲉ ϩⲛ̄ⲛⲟⲩⲛⲟϭ ⲛ̄ⲇⲩⲛⲁⲙⲓⲥ ϣⲓⲛⲁ ϫⲉⲛⲉⲛ̄ⲗⲏⲥⲧⲏⲥ ϩⲉ ⲉϩⲓⲏ ⲉⲉⲓ ϣⲁⲣⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲉⲡⲉⲓⲧⲉⲭⲣⲉⲓⲁ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϭⲱϣⲧ⳿ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲏⲧⲥ︦ ⲥⲉⲛⲁϩⲉ · ⲉⲣⲟⲥ · ⲙⲁⲣⲉϥϣⲱⲡⲉ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲙⲏⲧⲉ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲟⲩⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲛⲉⲡⲓⲥⲧⲏⲙⲱⲛ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲣⲉⲡⲕⲁⲣⲡⲟⲥ ⲡⲱϩ ⲁϥⲉⲓ ϩⲛ̄ⲛⲟⲩϭⲉⲡⲏ ⲉⲡⲉϥⲁⲥϩ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲉϥϭⲓϫ ⲁϥϩⲁⲥϥ ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲟⲩⲛ̄ⲙⲁⲁϫⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟϥ ⲉⲥⲱⲧⲙ̄ ⲙⲁⲣⲉϥⲥⲱⲧⲙ̄

i18n.en: Mariham said to Jesus: Whom are your disciples like? He said: They are like little children who have settled in a field that is not theirs. When the owners of the field come, they will say, 'Release our field to us.' They strip naked in their presence in order to release it to them and give them their field. Therefore I say: If the master of the house knows that the thief is coming, he will keep watch before he comes and will not let him dig through into his house of his domain to carry away his goods. You, then, keep watch against the world. Gird your loins with great power, so that the robbers do not find a way to come to you, for the need you are watching out for, they will find it. Let there be among you a man of understanding. When the fruit ripened, he came in haste with his sickle in his hand; he reaped it. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.

notes.official:
**Mariham.** ⲙⲁⲣⲓϩⲁⲙ is kept in the manuscript's form; the text does not say which Mary. Most commentators identify her with Mary Magdalene (compare logion 114 and other early texts in which a Mariam questions Jesus).

**The householder.** ⲉⲡⲉϥⲏⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉ ⲧⲉϥⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ is rendered 'his house of his domain' (Lambdin). ⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ is the word rendered 'kingdom' elsewhere, here used of the householder's own property. ⲥⲉⲕⲁⲕⲁϩⲏⲩ 'they strip naked' anticipates logion 37. Compare Mt 24:43 / Lk 12:39 (the thief) and Mk 4:29 (the sickle).

**The robbers clause.** As written, ϫⲉⲛⲉⲛ̄ⲗⲏⲥⲧⲏⲥ has ⲛⲉ-, which the corpus tags as a preterite converter. The clause makes sense only if ⲛⲉ is read as the negative optative ⲛ̄ⲛⲉ- 'so that … not', which is how all standard translations take it (Lambdin: 'lest the robbers find a way'). The English prints the negative sense without brackets; see `logion-21-robbers-clause-and-chreia-thomas-woh`. In the next clause, ⲥⲉⲛⲁϩⲉ ⲉⲣⲟⲥ 'they will find it' has ⲧⲉⲭⲣⲉⲓⲁ 'the need' as its object; Lambdin paraphrases 'the difficulty which you expect will (surely) materialize'.

paragraphs.text: ⲁⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲛⲁⲩ ⲁϩⲛ̄ⲕⲟⲩⲉⲓ ⲉⲩϫⲓⲉⲣⲱⲧⲉ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉϥⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ϫⲉⲛⲉⲉⲓⲕⲟⲩⲉⲓ ⲉⲧϫⲓⲉⲣⲱⲧⲉ ⲉⲩⲧⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲛ ⲁⲛⲉⲧⲃⲏⲕ ⲉϩⲟⲩⲛ ⲁⲧⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ ⲡⲉϫⲁⲩ ⲛⲁϥ⳿ ϫⲉⲉⲉⲓⲉⲛⲟ ⲛ̄ⲕⲟⲩⲉⲓ ⲧⲛ̄ⲛⲁⲃⲱⲕ⳿ ⲉϩⲟⲩⲛ ⲉⲧⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓⲏ︤ⲥ︥ ⲛⲁⲩ ϫⲉϩⲟⲧⲁⲛ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲁⲣ̄ⲡⲥⲛⲁⲩ ⲟⲩⲁ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲁⲣ̄ⲡⲥⲁ ⲛϩⲟⲩⲛ ⲛ̄ⲑⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲥⲁ ⲛⲃⲟⲗ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲥⲁ ⲛⲃⲟⲗ ⲛ̄ⲑⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲥⲁ ⲛϩⲟⲩⲛ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲥⲁ ⲛⲧⲡⲉ ⲛ̄ⲑⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲥⲁ ⲙⲡⲓⲧⲛ̄ ⲁⲩⲱ ϣⲓⲛⲁ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁⲉⲓⲣⲉ ⲙ̄ⲫⲟ·ⲟⲩⲧ ⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲥϩⲓⲙⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲓⲟⲩⲁ ⲟⲩⲱⲧ · ϫⲉⲕⲁⲁⲥ ⲛⲉⲫⲟⲟⲩⲧ · ⲣ̄ϩⲟⲟⲩⲧ · ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲥϩⲓⲙⲉ ⲣ̄ⲥϩⲓⲙⲉ ϩⲟⲧⲁⲛ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲁⲉⲓⲣⲉ ⲛ̄ϩⲛ̄ⲃⲁⲗ ⲉⲡⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲃⲁⲗ · ⲁⲩⲱ ⲟⲩϭⲓϫ⳿ ⲉⲡⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ⲛⲟⲩϭⲓϫ · ⲁⲩⲱ ⲟⲩ ⲉⲣⲏⲧⲉ ⲉⲡⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲉⲣⲏⲧⲉ ⲟⲩϩⲓⲕⲱⲛ · ⲉⲡⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩϩⲓⲕⲱⲛ ⲧⲟⲧⲉ ⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁⲃⲱⲕ̂ ⲉϩⲟⲩⲛ [ⲉⲧ]ⲙⲛ̄[ⲧⲉⲣ]ⲟ⳿

i18n.en: Jesus saw little ones being nursed. He said to his disciples: These little ones being nursed are like those who enter the kingdom. They said to him: Then shall we, being little ones, enter the kingdom? Jesus said to them: When you make the two one, and when you make the inside like the outside and the outside like the inside, and the upper side like the lower side, and so that you make the male and the female into the single one, so that the male will not be male and the female will not be female; when you make eyes in place of an eye, and a hand in place of a hand, and a foot in place of a foot, an image in place of an image, then you will enter [the kingdom].

notes.official:
**Making the two one.** The 'when you make' clauses have close parallels in 2 Clement 12.2 and in a saying that Clement of Alexandria quotes from the Gospel of the Egyptians (Strom. 3.13.92): the two become one, the outside as the inside, the male with the female neither male nor female. Compare Gen 1:27 and Gal 3:28. ⲙ̄ⲡⲓⲟⲩⲁ ⲟⲩⲱⲧ 'the single one' has the demonstrative article. 'And so that you make' keeps ϣⲓⲛⲁ with the form Dilley tags as optative / 'second future'. ⲟⲩϩⲓⲕⲱⲛ 'an image' recurs at 50, 83 and 84.

**Restoration and source notes.** ⲉϩⲟⲩⲛ [ⲉⲧ]ⲙⲛ̄[ⲧⲉⲣ]ⲟ is partly restored, hence 'enter [the kingdom]'. The lemma aid counts six supplied spans where `text` shows two bracketed spans. The diplomatic ⲙ̄ⲫⲟ·ⲟⲩⲧ has a middle dot inside the word, either the manuscript's punctuation or an encoding artefact. Neither affects the English.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉϯⲛⲁⲥⲉⲧⲡⲧⲏⲛⲉ ⲟⲩⲁ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ϣⲟ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲥⲛⲁⲩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲃⲁ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲥⲉⲛⲁⲱϩⲉ ⲉⲣⲁⲧⲟⲩ ⲉⲩⲟ ⲟⲩⲁ ⲟⲩⲱⲧ ·

i18n.en: Jesus said: I will choose you, one out of a thousand and two out of ten thousand, and they will stand as a single one.

notes.official: 'They will stand as a single one' uses the same ⲟⲩⲁ ⲟⲩⲱⲧ as 4 and 22. The shift from 'you' to 'they' is in the Coptic.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲛⲉϥⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ϫⲉⲙⲁⲧⲥⲉⲃⲟⲛ⳿ ⲉⲡⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ ⲉⲧⲕⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ ⲉⲡⲉⲓⲧⲁⲛⲁⲅⲕⲏ ⲉⲣⲟⲛ ⲧⲉ ⲉⲧⲣⲛ̄ϣⲓⲛⲉ ⲛⲥⲱϥ⳿ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ̂ ⲛⲁⲩ ϫⲉⲡⲉⲧⲉⲩⲛ̄ⲙⲁⲁϫⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟϥ ⲙⲁⲣⲉϥ · ⲥⲱⲧⲙ̄ ⲟⲩⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ⳿ ϣⲟⲟⲡ · ⲙ̄ⲫⲟⲩⲛ ⲛ̄ⲛⲟⲩⲣ̄ⲙ̄ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ ⲁⲩⲱ ϥⲣ̄ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ ⲉⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ ⲧⲏⲣϥ⳿ ⲉϥⲧⲙ̄ⲣ̄ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ⳿ ⲟⲩⲕⲁⲕⲉ ⲡⲉ

i18n.en: His disciples said: Show us the place where you are, for it is necessary for us to seek it. He said to them: Whoever has ears, let him hear. There is light within a man of light, and he gives light to the whole world. If he does not give light, it is darkness.

notes.official: ⲙⲁⲧⲥⲉⲃⲟⲛ ⲉⲡⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ can mean 'show us' or 'teach us about' the place; 'Show us' follows Lambdin. In ϥⲣ̄ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ 'he gives light' the masculine subject can be the man of light or the light itself (ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ is masculine), so 'it shines on the whole world' is equally possible. Compare Mt 6:22-23 / Lk 11:34-36 and Mt 5:14. P.Oxy. 655 preserves only traces of this saying.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲙⲉⲣⲉⲡⲉⲕⲥⲟⲛ ⲛ̄ⲑⲉ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲕⲯⲩⲭⲏ ⲉⲣⲓⲧⲏⲣⲉⲓ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟϥ ⲛ̄ⲑⲉ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲗⲟⲩ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲕ⳿ⲃⲁⲗ⳿

i18n.en: Jesus said: Love your brother as your soul; guard him like the pupil of your eye.

notes.official: 'As your soul' keeps ⲯⲩⲭⲏ. The idiom is reflexive ('as yourself', compare Lev 19:18; Mk 12:31), and 'like the pupil of your eye' recalls Deut 32:10 and Ps 17:8. The English does not harmonise to the synoptic 'as yourself'.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲡϫⲏ ⲉⲧϩⲙ̄ⲡⲃⲁⲗ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲕ⳿ⲥⲟⲛ ⲕⲛⲁⲩ ⲉⲣⲟϥ̂ ⲡⲥⲟⲉⲓ ⲇⲉ ⲉⲧϩⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲕⲃⲁⲗ⳿ ⲕⲛⲁⲩ ⲁⲛ ⲉⲣⲟϥ⳿ ϩⲟⲧⲁⲛ ⲉⲕϣⲁⲛⲛⲟⲩϫⲉ ⲙⲡⲥⲟⲉⲓ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲙⲡⲉⲕ⳿ⲃⲁⲗ · ⲧⲟⲧⲉ ⲕⲛⲁⲛⲁⲩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲉⲛⲟⲩϫⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡϫⲏ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲃⲁⲗ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲕⲥⲟⲛ

i18n.en: Jesus said: The speck that is in your brother's eye you see, but the beam that is in your own eye you do not see. When you cast the beam out of your own eye, then you will see clearly to cast the speck out of your brother's eye.

notes.official: Compare Mt 7:3-5 / Lk 6:41-42. P.Oxy. 1 begins with the end of this saying ('… and then you will see clearly to cast out the speck that is in your brother's eye'), in agreement with the Coptic.

paragraphs.text: ⲉⲧⲉ⟨ⲧⲛ̄⟩ⲧⲙ̄ⲣ̄ⲛⲏⲥⲧⲉⲩⲉ ⲉⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ ⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁϩⲉ ⲁⲛ⳿ ⲉⲧⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲧⲙ̄ⲉⲓⲣⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲥⲁⲙⲃⲁⲧⲟⲛ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁⲃ⳿ⲃⲁⲧⲟⲛ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁⲛⲁⲩ ⲁⲛ ⲉⲡⲉⲓⲱⲧ

i18n.en: If you do not fast from the world, you will not find the kingdom. If you do not keep the Sabbath as Sabbath, you will not see the Father.

notes.official:
**No introductory formula.** The Coptic has no ⲡⲉϫⲉ ⲓ︤ⲥ︥; the Greek (P.Oxy. 1.4-11) has λέγει Ἰη(σοῦ)ς, and the English does not supply it. The Greek also reads 'the kingdom of God' where the Coptic has 'the kingdom'.

'Fast from the world' renders ⲛⲏⲥⲧⲉⲩⲉ ⲉⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ (Greek νηστεύσητε τὸν κόσμον). 'Keep the Sabbath as Sabbath' renders ⲉⲓⲣⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲥⲁⲙⲃⲁⲧⲟⲛ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁⲃⲃⲁⲧⲟⲛ (Greek σαββατίσητε τὸ σάββατον). Whether the saying requires literal Sabbath observance, treats the whole week as Sabbath, or uses 'Sabbath' figuratively is debated, and the English leaves it open. ⲉⲧⲉ⟨ⲧⲛ̄⟩ contains an editorial addition, rendered silently.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲁⲉⲓⲱϩⲉ ⲉⲣⲁⲧ⳿ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲙⲏⲧⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁⲉⲓⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛⲁⲩ ϩⲛ̄ⲥⲁⲣⲝ ⲁⲉⲓϩⲉ ⲉⲣⲟⲟⲩ ⲧⲏⲣⲟⲩ ⲉⲩⲧⲁϩⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲓϩⲉ ⲉⲗⲁⲁⲩ ⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧⲟⲩ ⲉϥⲟⲃⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁⲧⲁⲯⲩⲭⲏ ϯⲧⲕⲁⲥ ⲉϫⲛ̄ⲛ̄ϣⲏⲣⲉ ⲛ̄ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ ϫⲉϩⲛ̄ⲃⲗ︦ⲗⲉⲉⲩ ⲉ ⲛⲉ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲟⲩϩⲏⲧ⳿ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲥⲉⲛⲁⲩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲁⲛ ϫⲉⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲩⲉⲓ ⲉⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ ⲉⲩϣⲟⲩⲉⲓⲧ⳿ · ⲉⲩϣⲓⲛⲉ ⲟⲛ ⲉⲧⲣⲟⲩⲉⲓ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ ⲉⲩϣⲟⲩⲉⲓⲧ⳿ ⲡⲗⲏⲛ ⲧⲉⲛⲟⲩ ⲥⲉⲧⲟϩⲉ ϩⲟⲧⲁⲛ ⲉⲩϣⲁⲛⲛⲉϩⲡⲟⲩⲏⲣⲡ⳿ ⲧⲟⲧⲉ ⲥⲉⲛⲁⲣ̄ⲙⲉⲧⲁⲛⲟⲉⲓ

i18n.en: Jesus said: I stood in the midst of the world, and I appeared to them in flesh. I found all of them drunk; I found none of them thirsty. And my soul was pained for the sons of men, because they are blind in their heart and do not see that they came into the world empty; empty they also seek to leave the world. But now they are drunk. When they shake off their wine, then they will repent.

notes.official: 'I appeared to them in flesh' (ϩⲛ̄ⲥⲁⲣⲝ) agrees with ἐν σαρκί in P.Oxy. 1.11-21, and 'the sons of men' keeps its υἱοῖς τῶν ἀνθρώπων. The figure who comes into the world and finds people unreceptive recalls the Jewish wisdom tradition (1 Enoch 42; Sir 24) and Jn 1:10-11. 'My soul' renders ⲯⲩⲭⲏ as at 25.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲉϣϫⲉⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲧⲥⲁⲣⲝ⳿ ϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲉⲧⲃⲉⲡⲛ︤ⲁ︥ ⲟⲩϣⲡⲏⲣⲉ ⲧⲉ ⲉϣϫⲉ ⲡⲛ︤ⲁ︥ ⲇⲉ ⲉⲧⲃⲉⲡⲥⲱⲙⲁ ⲟⲩϣⲡⲏⲣⲉ ⲛ̄ϣⲡⲏⲣⲉ ⲡⲉ ⲁⲗⲗⲁ ⲁⲛⲟⲕ⳿ ϯⲣ̄ϣⲡⲏⲣⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲁⲉⲓ ϫⲉⲡⲱ[ⲥ] ⲁⲧⲉⲉⲓⲛⲟϭ ⲙ̄ⲙ︤ⲛ︥︤ⲧ︥ⲣⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲟ ⲁⲥⲟⲩⲱϩ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲉⲓⲙ︤ⲛ︥︤ⲧ︥ϩⲏⲕⲉ

i18n.en: Jesus said: If the flesh came into being because of spirit, it is a wonder. But if spirit came into being because of the body, it is a wonder of wonders. But as for me, I marvel at this: [how] this great wealth has made its home in this poverty.

notes.official: 'A wonder … a wonder of wonders' (ϣⲡⲏⲣⲉ) uses the root of 'he will marvel' in logion 2. ⲥⲁⲣⲝ 'flesh' and ⲥⲱⲙⲁ 'body' are kept distinct, and ⲡⲛ︤ⲁ︥ is the human spirit, in lower case. ⲡⲱ[ⲥ] 'how' is partly restored, hence '[how]'. The end of the saying, with 'this poverty', survives in P.Oxy. 1.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲡⲙⲁ ⲉⲩⲛ̄ϣⲟⲙⲧ ⲛⲛⲟⲩⲧⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ ϩⲛ̄ⲛⲟⲩⲧⲉ ⲛⲉ ⲡⲙⲁ ⲉⲩⲛ̄ⲥⲛⲁⲩ ⲏ ⲟⲩⲁ ⲁⲛⲟⲕ⳿ ϯϣⲟⲟⲡ⳿ ⲛⲙⲙⲁϥ ·

i18n.en: Jesus said: Where there are three gods, they are gods. Where there are two or one, I am with him.

notes.official: **The crux.** The Coptic reads 'Where there are three gods, they are gods. Where there are two or one, I am with him.' Taken as it stands, the first sentence is nearly tautological, and many scholars suspect corruption. The Greek (P.Oxy. 1.23-30) differs: 'Where there are [three], they are [gods / without God]' (the key word is restored as θεοί or ἄθεοι), 'and where there is one alone, I say, I am with him', followed by 'Lift the stone and you will find me there; split the wood and I am there', which the Coptic places in logion 77. Compare Mt 18:20. The WoH text prints the manuscript reading; emendations toward the Greek are conjectures.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲙⲛ̄ⲡⲣⲟⲫⲏⲧⲏⲥ ϣⲏⲡ · ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲉϥϯⲙⲉ ⲙⲁⲣⲉⲥⲟⲉⲓⲛ ⲣ̄ⲑⲉⲣⲁⲡⲉⲩⲉ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲧ⳿ⲥⲟⲟⲩⲛ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟϥ⳿

i18n.en: Jesus said: No prophet is accepted in his village; a physician does not heal those who know him.

notes.official: Compare Mk 6:4 and Lk 4:23-24. The Greek (P.Oxy. 1.30-35) has ἐν τῇ πατρίδι αὐτοῦ 'in his homeland' where the Coptic has ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲉϥϯⲙⲉ 'in his village', and it agrees on the physician.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲟⲩⲡⲟⲗⲓⲥ ⲉⲩⲕⲱⲧ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲥ ϩⲓϫⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲧⲟⲟⲩ ⲉϥϫⲟⲥⲉ ⲉⲥⲧⲁϫⲣⲏⲩ ⲙⲛ̄ϭⲟⲙ ⲛ̄ⲥϩⲉ ⲟⲩⲇⲉ ⲥⲛⲁϣϩⲱⲡ⳿ ⲁⲛ

i18n.en: Jesus said: A city being built on a high mountain and fortified cannot fall, nor can it be hidden.

notes.official:
Compare Mt 5:14. The Greek (P.Oxy. 1.36-41) agrees in substance.

**Source note.** The diplomatic text ends ⲥⲛⲁϣϩⲱⲡ ⲁⲛ (negative ⲁⲛ), which the corpus normalises to ⲟⲛ 'again, either'. With ⲟⲩⲇⲉ the sense 'nor can it be hidden' is the same on either reading.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲡⲉⲧ⳿ⲕⲛⲁⲥⲱⲧⲙ̄ ⲉⲣⲟϥ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲕ⳿ⲙⲁⲁϫⲉ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲉⲙⲁⲁϫⲉ ⲧⲁϣⲉⲟⲉⲓϣ⳿ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟϥ · ϩⲓϫⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲧⲛϫⲉⲛⲉⲡⲱⲣ⳿ ⲙⲁⲣⲉⲗⲁⲁⲩ⳿ · ⲅⲁⲣ ϫⲉⲣⲉϩⲏⲃ︤ⲥ︥ ⲛ̄ϥ⳿ⲕⲁⲁϥ · ϩⲁⲙⲁⲁϫⲉ ⲟⲩⲇⲉ ⲙⲁϥⲕⲁⲁϥ · ϩⲙ̄ⲙⲁ ⲉϥϩⲏⲡ⳿ · ⲁⲗⲗⲁ ⲉϣⲁⲣⲉϥⲕⲁⲁϥ⳿ ϩⲓϫⲛ̄ⲧⲗⲩⲭⲛⲓⲁ ϫⲉⲕⲁⲁⲥ ⲟⲩⲟⲛ ⲛⲓⲙ⳿ ⲉⲧⲃⲏⲕ⳿ ⲉϩⲟⲩⲛ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲛⲏⲩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲉⲩⲛⲁⲛⲁⲩ ⲁⲡⲉϥⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ

i18n.en: Jesus said: What you will hear in your ear, in the other ear proclaim it upon your rooftops. For no one lights a lamp and puts it under a measure, nor does he put it in a hidden place; rather, he sets it on the lampstand, so that everyone who comes in and goes out will see its light.

notes.official: **Two cruxes.** (1) 'In your ear, in the other ear': ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲉⲙⲁⲁϫⲉ may be a scribal repetition, or may mean 'into another's ear', i.e. pass on what you hear. The Greek (P.Oxy. 1.41-42) has 'in your one ear', which supports a contrast between two ears, so the English keeps the manuscript sequence. (2) ⲙⲁⲁϫⲉ means both 'ear' and a dry 'measure', and Thomas uses both senses in one saying. ϩⲁⲙⲁⲁϫⲉ is rendered 'under a measure' so that the pun can be seen (Lambdin: 'bushel'; matthew-woh at Mt 5:15: 'basket' for μόδιος). Compare Mt 10:27 and Mt 5:15 / Lk 11:33.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲟⲩⲃⲗ︦ⲗⲉ ⲉϥϣⲁⲛ⳿ⲥⲱⲕ⳿ ϩⲏⲧϥ⳿ ⲛ̄ⲛⲟⲩⲃⲗ︦ⲗⲉ ϣⲁⲩϩⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲥⲛⲁⲩ⳿ · ⲉⲡⲉⲥⲏⲧ · ⲉⲩϩⲓⲉⲓⲧ⳿ ·

i18n.en: Jesus said: If a blind man leads a blind man, both of them fall down into a pit.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲙⲛ̄ϭⲟⲙ⳿ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲟⲩⲁ ⲃⲱⲕ⳿ ⲉϩⲟⲩⲛ ⲉⲡⲏⲉⲓ ⲙ̄ⲡϫⲱⲱⲣⲉ ⲛ̄ϥϫⲓⲧϥ⳿ ⲛ̄ϫⲛⲁϩ ⲉⲓⲙⲏⲧⲓ ⲛ̄ϥⲙⲟⲩⲣ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉϥϭⲓϫ⳿ ⲧⲟⲧⲉ ϥⲛⲁⲡⲱⲱⲛⲉ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉϥⲏⲉⲓ

i18n.en: Jesus said: It is not possible for anyone to enter the house of the strong man and take it by force unless he binds his hands; then he will ransack his house.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲙⲛ̄ϥⲓⲣⲟⲟⲩϣ ϫⲓ(ⲛ)ϩⲧⲟⲟⲩⲉ ϣⲁⲣⲟⲩϩⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ϫⲓⲛϩⲓⲣⲟⲩϩⲉ ϣⲁϩⲧⲟⲟⲩⲉ ϫⲉⲟⲩ ⲡⲉ⟨ⲧ⟩ⲉⲧⲛⲁⲧⲁⲁϥ ϩⲓⲱⲧ⳿ⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄

i18n.en: Jesus said: Do not be anxious from morning until evening and from evening until morning about what you will put on.

notes.official:
**Short Coptic, long Greek.** The Coptic has only the core prohibition about clothing. The Greek (P.Oxy. 655 col. i.1-17) is much longer: it adds food, the lilies 'which neither card nor spin', a question about having one garment, 'who could add to your stature?', and 'he himself will give you your garment'. Compare Mt 6:25-34 / Lk 12:22-31. The WoH text follows the Coptic.

ⲙⲛ̄ϥⲓⲣⲟⲟⲩϣ is a Lycopolitan prohibitive. ϫⲓ(ⲛ) and ⲡⲉ⟨ⲧ⟩ contain editorially supplied letters, rendered silently.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲛⲉϥⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ϫⲉⲁϣ ⲛ̄ϩⲟⲟⲩ ⲉⲕⲛⲁⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛⲁⲛ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁϣ ⲛ̄ϩⲟⲟⲩ ⲉⲛⲁⲛⲁⲩ ⲉⲣⲟⲕ⳿ ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉϩⲟⲧⲁⲛ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲁⲕⲉⲕⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄ ⲉϩⲏⲩ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲓⲡⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϥⲓ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲧⲏⲛ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲕⲁⲁⲩ ϩⲁⲡⲉⲥⲏⲧ⳿ · ⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲉⲣⲏⲧⲉ ⲛ̄ⲑⲉ ⲛ̄ⲛⲓⲕⲟⲩⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ϣⲏⲣⲉ ϣⲏⲙ⳿ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϫⲟⲡϫ︦ⲡ︦ · ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲟⲩ ⲧⲟⲧ[ⲉ] [ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄]ⲁⲛⲁⲩ ⲉⲡϣⲏⲣⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲟⲛϩ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁⲣ̄ϩⲟⲧⲉ ⲁⲛ

i18n.en: His disciples said: On what day will you appear to us, and on what day will we see you? Jesus said: When you strip yourselves naked without being ashamed, and take your garments and lay them under your feet like little children and trample on them, [then you will] see the son of the living one, and you will not be afraid.

notes.official:
**Undressing without shame.** The image recalls Gen 2:25 and 3:7 and the 'garment of shame' saying quoted from the Gospel of the Egyptians (Clement, Strom. 3.13.92); compare logion 21. 'The son of the living one' is lower case (see `etonh-the-living-lowercase-thomas-woh`). It is not the 'Son of Man' phrase, which Thomas uses only at 86. The Greek (P.Oxy. 655 col. i.17-ii.1) agrees broadly but is fragmentary.

**Restoration.** ⲧⲟⲧ[ⲉ] [ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄]ⲁⲛⲁⲩ is partly restored, hence '[then you will] see'.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉϩⲁϩ ⲛ̄ⲥⲟⲡ · ⲁⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲣ̄ⲉⲡⲓⲑⲩⲙⲉⲓ ⲉⲥⲱⲧⲙ̄ ⲁⲛⲉⲉⲓϣⲁϫⲉ ⲛⲁⲉⲓ⳿ · ⲉϯϫⲱ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲟⲩ ⲛⲏⲧⲛ̄ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲏⲧⲛ̄ ⲕⲉⲟⲩⲁ ⲉⲥⲟⲧⲙⲟⲩ ⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲟⲧϥ︦ ⲟⲩⲛ̄ϩⲛ̄ϩⲟⲟⲩ ⲛⲁϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲓⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ⲥⲱⲉⲓ ⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁϩⲉ ⲁⲛ⳿ ⲉⲣⲟⲉⲓ⳿

i18n.en: Jesus said: Many times you have desired to hear these sayings that I am speaking to you, and you have no one else from whom to hear them. There will be days when you will seek me and you will not find me.

notes.official: Compare Mt 13:17 / Lk 10:24 (many desired to hear) and Jn 7:34 ('you will seek me and will not find me'). P.Oxy. 655 preserves only scraps of this saying; the usual restoration agrees with the Coptic.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲙ̄ⲫⲁⲣⲓⲥⲁⲓⲟⲥ ⲙⲛ̄ⲛⲅⲣⲁⲙⲙⲁⲧⲉⲩⲥ ⲁⲩϫⲓ ⲛ̄ϣⲁϣⲧ⳿ · ⲛ̄ⲧⲅⲛⲱⲥⲓⲥ ⲁⲩϩⲟⲡⲟⲩ ⲟⲩⲧⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲟⲩⲃⲱⲕ⳿ ⲉϩⲟⲩⲛ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲛⲉⲧⲟⲩⲱϣ ⲉⲃⲱⲕ⳿ ⲉϩⲟⲩⲛ ⲙ̄ⲡⲟⲩⲕⲁⲁⲩ ⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲇⲉ ϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲙ̄ⲫⲣⲟⲛⲓⲙⲟⲥ ⲛ̄ⲑⲉ ⲛ̄ⲛϩⲟϥ⳿ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲛ̄ⲁⲕⲉⲣⲁⲓⲟⲥ ⲛ̄ⲑⲉ ⲛ̄ⲛ̄ϭⲣⲟⲙ⳿ⲡⲉ

i18n.en: Jesus said: The Pharisees and the scribes have taken the keys of knowledge and have hidden them. They did not go in, nor did they let those who wish to go in. You, however, be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.

notes.official:
**Greek witness.** Logion 39 is the last saying with a Greek overlap in P.Oxy. 655 (col. ii). The extant letters are few and most of the Greek is restored (Attridge in Layton ed. 1989). The usual restoration agrees with the Coptic. The participle sometimes restored as 'those who are entering' (cf. Lk 11:52 τοὺς εἰσερχομένους) stands largely on restored letters, so it establishes no difference from the Coptic 'those who wish to go in'. The line translates the Coptic (see `coptic-base-text-and-oxyrhynchus-greek-witnesses-convention-thomas-woh`).

**'The keys of knowledge'.** ⲅⲛⲱⲥⲓⲥ, its only occurrence in Thomas, is translated, not transliterated (see `gnosis-knowledge-thomas-woh`). The Coptic has plural 'keys' where Lk 11:52 has 'the key of knowledge'. ⲁⲩϩⲟⲡⲟⲩ 'they hid them' is the active verb whose stative gives the 'hidden' sayings of the incipit. The last sentence matches Mt 10:16 ('wise as serpents and innocent as doves'); the woe against the Pharisees and scribes compares with Mt 23:13.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲟⲩⲃⲉⲛⲉⲗⲟⲟⲗⲉ ⲁⲩⲧⲟϭⲥ ⲙ̄ⲡⲥⲁ ⲛⲃⲟⲗ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲓⲱⲧ⳿ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲉⲥⲧⲁ⳿ϫⲣⲏⲩ ⲁⲛ ⲥⲉⲛⲁⲡⲟⲣⲕⲥ︦ ϩⲁⲧⲉⲥⲛⲟⲩⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ⲥⲧⲁⲕⲟ

i18n.en: Jesus said: A grapevine has been planted outside the Father, and since it is not established, it will be pulled up by its root and will perish.

notes.official: Compare Mt 15:13 ('every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted'). In Thomas the vine is planted 'outside the Father', and the circumstantial ⲉⲥⲧⲁϫⲣⲏⲩ ⲁⲛ 'it not being established' gives the reason it will be uprooted.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲡⲉⲧⲉⲩⲛⲧⲁϥ · ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲉϥ⳿ϭⲓϫ ⲥⲉⲛⲁϯ ⲛⲁϥ⳿ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲁϥ ⲡⲕⲉϣⲏⲙ ⲉⲧⲟⲩⲛ̄ⲧⲁϥ⳿ ⲥⲉⲛⲁϥⲓⲧϥ̄ ⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲟⲧϥ̄

i18n.en: Jesus said: Whoever has in his hand, it will be given to him; and whoever does not have, even the little that he has will be taken from him.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛⲣ̄ⲡⲁⲣⲁⲅⲉ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Become passers-by.

notes.official: **The shortest saying.** ϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲣ̄ⲡⲁⲣⲁⲅⲉ is an imperative 'become' with a circumstantial of the Greek loan παράγειν. The line reads it predicatively, as the standard translation does (Lambdin, 'Become passers-by'). παράγειν means both 'pass by' and 'pass away' (1 Cor 7:31, of the form of this world). The saying has been read as a call to detachment from the world and as a call to an itinerant life. An adverbial reading, 'Come into being as you pass away', is also argued. The English keeps 'passers-by', which leaves those readings open (see `parage-passers-by-logion-42-thomas-woh`).

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲁⲩ ⲛⲁϥ⳿ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲛⲉϥ⳿ⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ϫⲉⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲕⲛⲓⲙ⳿ ⲉⲕϫⲱ ⲛ̄ⲛⲁⲓ̈ ⲛⲁⲛ⳿ ϩⲛ̄ⲛⲉϯϫⲱ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲟⲩ ⲛⲏⲧⲛ̄ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲉⲓⲙⲉ ⲁⲛ ϫⲉⲁⲛⲟⲕ⳿ⲛⲓⲙ ⲁⲗⲗⲁ ⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲁⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲛ̄ⲑⲉ ⲛ̄ⲛⲓⲓ̈ⲟⲩⲇⲁⲓⲟⲥ ϫⲉⲥⲉⲙⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡϣⲏⲛ ⲥⲉⲙⲟⲥⲧⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉϥⲕⲁⲣⲡⲟⲥ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲥⲉⲙⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲁⲣⲡⲟⲥ ⲥⲉⲙⲟⲥⲧⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡϣⲏⲛ

i18n.en: His disciples said to him: Who are you, that you say these things to us? From what I say to you, you do not know who I am. But you have become like the Jews: they love the tree, they hate its fruit; and they love the fruit, they hate the tree.

notes.official:
**No speech formula.** After the disciples' question, Jesus's answer follows with no ⲡⲉϫⲉ ⲓ︤ⲥ︥. Some translations supply '⟨Jesus said to them⟩'. Under the register convention the English supplies nothing, as at logion 27. The change of speaker is clear from the first-person singular 'what I say to you'. Compare Jn 8:25 ('Who are you?').

**'The Jews'.** ⲛ̄ⲛⲓⲓ̈ⲟⲩⲇⲁⲓⲟⲥ is the only occurrence of the ethnonym in Thomas. It is rendered 'the Jews', as in the standard translations; 'the Judeans' is the alternative proposed in part of NT scholarship (see `ioudaioi-the-jews-thomas-woh`). The saying is polemical, and the translation does not soften it. The tree-and-fruit image compares with Mt 7:16-20 and 12:33.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲡⲉⲧⲁϫⲉⲟⲩⲁ ⲁⲡⲉⲓⲱⲧ⳿ ⲥⲉⲛⲁⲕⲱ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛⲁϥ⳿ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲉⲧⲁϫⲉⲟⲩⲁ ⲉⲡϣⲏⲣⲉ ⲥⲉⲛⲁⲕⲱ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛⲁϥ⳿ ⲡⲉⲧⲁϫⲉⲟⲩⲁ ⲇⲉ ⲁⲡⲡⲛ︤ⲁ︥ ⲉⲧⲟⲩⲁⲁⲃ ⲥⲉⲛⲁⲕⲱ ⲁⲛ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛⲁϥ⳿ ⲟⲩⲧⲉ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲁϩ ⲟⲩⲧⲉ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲡⲉ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Whoever blasphemes against the Father, he will be forgiven; and whoever blasphemes against the Son, he will be forgiven; but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, he will not be forgiven, neither on earth nor in heaven.

notes.official: **The triad.** Thomas has Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Mt 12:31-32 (compare Mk 3:28-29; Lk 12:10) contrasts blasphemy against the Son of Man with blasphemy against the Spirit. 'The Son' is capitalised because the triad gives the divine referent; this is outside the filial formulas governed by `shere-son-child-thomas-woh` (see `son-and-holy-spirit-triad-logion-44-thomas-woh`). The impersonal 'they will forgive him' is rendered by the passive 'he will be forgiven'. 'Neither on earth nor in heaven' uses 'heaven' for ⲧⲡⲉ in a cosmological pair, under the sky/heaven context rule.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲙⲁⲩϫⲉⲗⲉⲉⲗⲟⲟⲗⲉ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ϣⲟⲛⲧⲉ ⲟⲩⲧⲉ ⲙⲁⲩⲕⲱⲧϥ⳿ⲕⲛ̄ⲧⲉ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ⲥⲣ̄ϭⲁⲙⲟⲩⲗ⳿ ⲙⲁⲩϯⲕⲁⲣⲡⲟⲥ ⲅⲁⲣ [ⲟⲩⲁ]ⲅⲁⲑⲟⲥ ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ ϣⲁϥⲉⲓⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲁⲅⲁⲑⲟⲛ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲙⲡⲉϥⲉϩⲟ ⲟⲩⲕⲁ[ⲕⲟ]ⲥ ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ ϣⲁϥⲉⲓⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ϩⲛ̄ⲡⲟⲛⲏⲣⲟⲛ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲉϥⲉϩⲟ ⲉⲑⲟⲟⲩ ⲉⲧϩⲛ̄ⲡⲉϥϩⲏⲧ⳿ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲛ̄ϥϫⲱ ⲛ̄ϩⲛ̄ⲡⲟⲛⲏⲣⲟⲛ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲅⲁⲣ ϩⲙ̄ⲫⲟⲩⲟ ⲙⲫⲏⲧ⳿ ϣⲁϥ·ⲉⲓⲛⲉ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛ̄ϩⲛ̄ⲡⲟⲛⲏⲣⲟⲛ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Grapes are not harvested from thorns, nor are figs gathered from thistles, for they do not yield fruit. [A good] man brings forth good from his treasure; a [bad] man brings forth evil things from his bad treasure, which is in his heart, and he says evil things, for out of the abundance of the heart he brings forth evil things.

notes.official:
**Restoration.** [ⲟⲩⲁ]ⲅⲁⲑⲟⲥ and ⲟⲩⲕⲁ[ⲕⲟ]ⲥ are partly restored, hence '[A good] man' and 'a [bad] man'.

**'Bad' and 'evil things'.** Greek ⲕⲁⲕⲟⲥ and native ϩⲟⲟⲩ (diplomatic ⲉⲑⲟⲟⲩ, normalised ⲉⲧϩⲟⲟⲩ) are both 'bad'; substantival ⲡⲟⲛⲏⲣⲟⲛ is 'evil things' (see `kakos-poneron-hoou-bad-evil-thomas-woh`). Compare Mt 7:16 and Lk 6:44-45. Thomas has no 'mouth' in the last clause: out of the abundance of the heart the man brings forth evil things.

**Source note.** The `text` field has a middle dot inside a word (ϣⲁϥ·ⲉⲓⲛⲉ), as at THOM-22. The normalised layer keeps it. It has no effect on the reading.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉϫⲓⲛⲁⲇⲁⲙ ϣⲁⲓ̈ⲱϩⲁⲛⲛⲏⲥ ⲡⲃⲁⲡⲧⲓⲥⲧⲏⲥ ϩⲛ̄ⲛ̄ϫⲡⲟ ⲛ̄ⲛ̄ϩⲓⲟⲙⲉ ⲙⲛ̄ⲡⲉⲧϫⲟⲥⲉ ⲁⲓ̈ⲱϩⲁⲛⲛⲏⲥ ⲡⲃⲁⲡⲧⲓⲥⲧⲏⲥ ϣⲓⲛⲁ ϫⲉⲛⲟⲩⲱϭⲡ · ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲛⲉϥⲃⲁⲗ ⲁⲉⲓϫⲟⲟⲥ ⲇⲉ ϫⲉⲡⲉⲧⲛⲁϣⲱⲡⲉ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄ ⲉϥⲟ ⲛ̄ⲕⲟⲩⲉⲓ ϥⲛⲁⲥⲟⲩⲱⲛⲧⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ ⲁⲩⲱ ϥⲛⲁϫⲓⲥⲉ ⲁⲓ̈ⲱϩⲁⲛⲛⲏⲥ

i18n.en: Jesus said: From Adam to John the Baptist, among those born of women there is no one more exalted than John the Baptist, so that his eyes should not be lowered. But I have said: Whoever among you becomes a little one will know the kingdom and will be more exalted than John.

notes.official:
**The unwritten negative.** The diplomatic text reads ϣⲓⲛⲁ ϫⲉⲛⲟⲩⲱϭⲡ, with no negative ('so that his eyes will be broken'). The corpus normalises it to the negative optative ⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲩⲟⲩⲱϭⲡ, and the lemma aid counts a supplied span that `text` does not mark. As at THOM-21, the English follows the normalised reading and prints the negative without brackets. All standard translations do the same.

**'Lowered'.** ⲟⲩⲱϭⲡ means 'break'. 'Lowered' (Lambdin) takes 'his eyes should not be broken' as an idiom for casting down the eyes before a superior. This is an interpretation, which `logion-46-eyes-lowered-and-little-one-thomas-woh` marks as `inferred`. Compare Mt 11:11 and Lk 7:28. Thomas frames the comparison 'from Adam to John the Baptist', and 'becomes a little one' takes up the 'little ones' of logion 22.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲙⲛ̄ϭⲟⲙ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲟⲩⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲧⲉⲗⲟ ⲁϩⲧⲟ ⲥⲛⲁⲩ ⲛ̄ϥϫⲱⲗⲕ⳿ ⲙ̄ⲡⲓⲧⲉ ⲥⲛ̄ⲧⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲙⲛ̄ϭⲟⲙ⳿ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲟⲩϩⲙϩ︤ⲁ︥︤ⲗ︥ ϣⲙ̄ϣⲉϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ ⲥⲛⲁⲩ ⲏ ϥⲛⲁⲣ̄ⲧⲓⲙⲁ ⲙ̄ⲡⲟⲩⲁ · ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲕⲉⲟⲩⲁ ϥⲛⲁⲣ̄ϩⲩⲃⲣⲓⲍⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟϥ⳿ ⲙⲁⲣⲉⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲥⲉⲣ̄ⲡ ⲁⲥ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲩⲛⲟⲩ ⲛ̄ϥ⳿ⲉⲡⲓⲑⲩⲙⲉⲓ ⲁⲥⲱⲏⲣⲡ⳿ ⲃ︦ⲃⲣⲣⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲙⲁⲩⲛⲟⲩϫ⳿ⲏⲣⲡ⳿ ⲛ̄ⲃⲣ̄ⲣⲉ ⲉⲁⲥⲕⲟⲥ ⲛ̄ⲁⲥ ϫⲉⲕⲁⲁⲥ ⲛ̄ⲛⲟⲩⲡⲱϩ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲙⲁⲩⲛⲉϫ⳿ⲏⲣⲡ⳿ ⲛ̄ⲁⲥ ⲉⲁⲥⲕⲟⲥ ⲛ̄ⲃⲣ̄ⲣⲉ ϣⲓⲛⲁ ϫⲉⲛⲉϥⲧⲉⲕⲁϥ⳿ ⲙⲁⲩϫ︤ⲗ︥ϭⲧⲟⲉⲓⲥ ⲛ̄ⲁⲥ ⲁϣⲧⲏ(ⲛ) ⲛ̄ϣⲁⲉⲓ ⲉⲡⲉⲓⲟⲩⲛⲟⲩⲡⲱϩ ⲛⲁϣⲱⲡⲉ

i18n.en: Jesus said: It is impossible for a man to mount two horses and to stretch two bows; and it is impossible for a slave to serve two masters, or else he will honor the one and the other he will treat with contempt. No one drinks old wine and immediately desires to drink new wine. And new wine is not put into old wineskins, lest they burst; nor is old wine put into a new wineskin, lest it spoil it. An old patch is not sewn onto a new garment, since a tear would result.

notes.official:
**Order and wording.** The two horses and two bows have no synoptic counterpart. The slave who 'will honor the one and … treat the other with contempt' compares with Mt 6:24 and Lk 16:13, where the verbs are 'love' and 'hate'. Thomas has the old-wine saying of Lk 5:39 before the wineskins, and it adds the converse case (old wine into a new wineskin). The patch saying is reversed: in Thomas an old patch is sewn onto a new garment, while in Mk 2:21 and Lk 5:36 a new patch is put on an old garment. The English keeps Thomas's form.

ϩⲙϩⲁⲗ is 'slave' and ϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ 'master' (see `hmhal-slave-joeis-master-lord-thomas-woh`). ⲁϣⲧⲏ(ⲛ) 'garment' has an abbreviated letter supplied by the edition, rendered silently.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲉⲣϣⲁⲥⲛⲁⲩ ⲣ̄ⲉⲓⲣⲏⲛⲏ ⲙⲛ̄ⲛⲟⲩⲉⲣⲏⲩ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲓⲏⲉⲓ ⲟⲩⲱⲧ⳿ ⲥⲉⲛⲁϫⲟⲟⲥ ⲙ̄ⲡⲧⲁⲩ ϫⲉⲡⲱⲱⲛⲉ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲁⲩⲱ ϥⲛⲁⲡⲱⲱⲛⲉ

i18n.en: Jesus said: If two make peace with each other in this single house, they will say to the mountain, 'Move away,' and it will move away.

notes.official: 'This single house' renders ⲡⲉⲓⲏⲉⲓ ⲟⲩⲱⲧ, adjectival ⲟⲩⲱⲧ without ⲟⲩⲁ. The same word recurs in 'this single pearl' (THOM-76), and 'single' keeps the link with 'a single one' (see `oua-ouot-a-single-one-thomas-woh`). Compare Mt 18:19 and 17:20, and the doublet at logion 106.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉϩⲉⲛⲙⲁⲕⲁⲣⲓⲟⲥ ⲛⲉ ⲛⲙⲟⲛⲁⲭⲟⲥ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲉⲧⲥⲟⲧⲡ⳿ ϫⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁϩⲉ ⲁⲧⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ ϫⲉⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲧⲛ̄ ϩⲛ̄ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧⲥ︦ ⲡⲁⲗⲓⲛ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁⲃⲱⲕ⳿ ⲉⲙⲁⲩ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Blessed are the solitary and chosen ones, for you will find the kingdom; for you are from it, and it is there that you will go again.

notes.official:
**One group, not two.** The relative ⲉⲧⲥⲟⲧⲡ 'who are chosen' has no article of its own. It therefore qualifies ⲛ̄ⲙⲟⲛⲁⲭⲟⲥ rather than naming a second group. The draft's 'the solitary ones and the chosen' is changed to 'the solitary and chosen ones'. Lambdin likewise has 'the solitary and elect'. 'Chosen', not 'elect', keeps the link with the verb ⲥⲱⲧⲡ at logia 8 and 23 (see `sotp-chosen-thomas-woh`). 'Solitary' follows `monachos-solitary-thomas-woh`.

The plural ϩⲉⲛⲙⲁⲕⲁⲣⲓⲟⲥ ⲛⲉ is 'Blessed are'. The saying has no synoptic counterpart, so the overlay beatitude entry applies, not the central one. The focalising future ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁⲃⲱⲕ ⲉⲙⲁⲩ is rendered as a cleft: 'it is there that you will go again'.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲉⲩϣⲁⲛϫⲟⲟⲥ ⲛⲏⲧⲛ̄ ϫⲉⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲧⲱⲛ ϫⲟⲟⲥ ⲛⲁⲩ ϫⲉⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲛⲉⲓ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ ⲡⲙⲁ ⲉⲛⲧⲁⲡⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ ϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲓⲧⲟⲟⲧϥ⳿ ⲟⲩⲁⲁⲧϥ⳿ ⲁϥⲱϩ[ⲉ ⲉⲣⲁⲧϥ] ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁϥⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ ⲉ[ⲃ]ⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲩϩⲓⲕⲱⲛ ⲉⲩϣⲁϫⲟⲟⲥ ⲛⲏⲧⲛ̄ ϫⲉⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲡⲉ ϫⲟⲟⲥ ϫⲉⲁⲛⲟⲛ ⲛⲉϥϣⲏⲣⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁⲛⲟⲛ ⲛ̄ⲥⲱⲧⲡ⳿ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲓⲱⲧ ⲉⲧⲟⲛϩ ⲉⲩϣⲁⲛϫⲛⲉⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄ ϫⲉⲟⲩ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲙⲁⲉⲓⲛ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲉⲓⲱⲧ ⲉⲧϩⲛ̄ⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄ ϫⲟⲟⲥ ⲉⲣⲟⲟⲩ ϫⲉⲟⲩⲕⲓⲙ ⲡⲉ ⲙⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲁⲛⲁⲡⲁⲩⲥⲓⲥ

i18n.en: Jesus said: If they say to you, 'From where did you come into being?', say to them, 'We came from the light, the place where the light came into being by itself. It [stood] and [appeared] in their image.' If they say to you, 'Is it you?', say, 'We are its sons, and we are the chosen of the living Father.' If they ask you, 'What is the sign of your Father in you?', say to them, 'It is movement and repose.'

notes.official:
**Restoration.** ⲁϥⲱϩ[ⲉ ⲉⲣⲁⲧϥ] and ⲉ[ⲃ]ⲟⲗ are partly restored, so both English verbs are bracketed: 'It [stood] and [appeared]'. The bracket rule is mechanical, and it applies even where only one letter of the secure adverb ⲉⲃⲟⲗ is restored. ⲱϩⲉ ⲉⲣⲁⲧ= is literally 'stand'. Lambdin's 'established [itself]' interprets it.

**Pronouns.** 'It' takes the light as the subject of ⲁϥ-, and 'its sons' takes the light as the antecedent of ⲛⲉϥ- (Lambdin: 'its children'). 'Sons' follows the ratified filial rule. The plural possessive in ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲩϩⲓⲕⲱⲛ 'in their image' (normalised ⲧⲉⲩ-) has no stated antecedent, and the English leaves it unresolved. ϫⲉⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲡⲉ is the question 'Is it you?' (see `logion-50-light-and-interrogation-vocabulary-thomas-woh`).

**'Movement and repose'.** ⲕⲓⲙ is the verb of logion 19 ('trees that do not move'). The Greek loan ⲁⲛⲁⲡⲁⲩⲥⲓⲥ is 'repose' here and at 51 and 60, and native ⲙ̄ⲧⲟⲛ is 'rest' (61). The draft's 'rest' is changed so that 'the rest of the dead' (51) cannot be misread as 'the remainder' (see `kim-anapausis-mton-movement-repose-rest-thomas-woh`). In mainstream commentary the saying is read as a catechism of origin and return, with 'the light' as the realm from which the chosen come (compare logion 49).

**Wheel of Heaven reading (interpretive; not part of the translation).** The saying answers a question of origin ('From where did you come into being?') with a place, and says that the light 'appeared in their image', with a plural possessive that the text does not resolve. A Wheel of Heaven reader will notice that plural, which can be read alongside 'Let us make man in our image' (Gen 1:26) and the canon's teaching that humans were made in the image of the Elohim. The saying itself names no makers and no place in the sky, and the English does not resolve 'their'. Mainstream commentators already relate logion 50 to Genesis 1 (e.g. DeConick 2006); only reading 'their' as the Elohim is speculative. See `woh-reading-logion-50-origin-from-the-light-thomas-woh` (speculative).

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲁⲩ ⲛⲁ·ϥ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲛⲉϥⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ϫⲉⲁϣ ⲛ̄ϩⲟⲟⲩ ⲉⲧⲁⲛⲁⲡⲁⲩⲥⲓⲥ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲧⲙⲟⲟⲩⲧ⳿ ⲛⲁϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁϣ ⲛ̄ϩⲟⲟⲩ ⲉⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ ⲃ︦ⲃⲣ̄ⲣⲉ ⲛⲏⲩ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁⲩ ϫⲉⲧⲏ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϭⲱϣⲧ⳿ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲏⲧⲥ︦ ⲁⲥⲉⲓ ⲁⲗⲗⲁ ⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲥⲟⲟⲩⲛ ⲁⲛ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲥ

i18n.en: His disciples said to him: On what day will the repose of the dead come about, and on what day is the new world coming? He said to them: What you are watching out for has come, but you do not know it.

notes.official:
**'The repose of the dead'.** The disciples take up the ⲁⲛⲁⲡⲁⲩⲥⲓⲥ of logion 50. The manuscript reads ⲁⲛⲁⲡⲁⲩⲥⲓⲥ, and the conjecture that 'resurrection' (ἀνάστασις) stood behind it has no support in the Coptic witness, so it is not printed. 'Repose' avoids the English ambiguity of 'the rest of the dead' (see `kim-anapausis-mton-movement-repose-rest-thomas-woh`). 'Watching out for' repeats the rendering of the same construction at THOM-21 (see `goosht-look-watch-thomas-woh`).

**Source note.** The diplomatic ⲉⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ is normalised to ⲉⲣⲉⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ. The `text` field has a middle dot inside ⲛⲁ·ϥ, which has no effect on the reading.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲁⲩ ⲛⲁϥ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲛⲉϥⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ϫⲉϫⲟⲩⲧⲁϥⲧⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲣⲟⲫⲏⲧⲏⲥ ⲁⲩϣⲁϫⲉ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲓⲥⲣⲁⲏⲗ⳿ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁⲩϣⲁϫⲉ ⲧⲏⲣⲟⲩ ϩⲣⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧⲕ⳿ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁⲩ ϫⲉⲁⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲕⲱ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲟⲛϩ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲙ̄ⲧⲟ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲁϫⲉ ϩⲁⲛⲉⲧⲙⲟⲟⲩⲧ⳿

i18n.en: His disciples said to him: Twenty-four prophets spoke in Israel, and all of them spoke in you. He said to them: You have left aside the living one in your presence, and you have spoken about the dead.

notes.official: 'Twenty-four' matches the count of the books of the Hebrew scriptures in 4 Ezra 14:45. ϩⲣⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧⲕ is literally 'in you'. It may mean that the prophets spoke about Jesus or that they spoke through him, and the English keeps 'in you' (see `logion-52-twenty-four-prophets-thomas-woh`). Jesus's answer is quoted in a similar form by Augustine (Contra adversarium legis et prophetarum 2.4.14). 'The living one' is lower case.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲁⲩ ⲛⲁϥ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲛⲉϥⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ϫⲉⲡⲥⲃ︦ⲃⲉ ⲣ̄ⲱⲫⲉⲗⲉⲓ ⲏ ⟨ⲙ̄⟩ⲙⲟⲛ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ⳿ ⲛⲁⲩ ϫⲉⲛⲉϥⲣ̄ⲱⲫⲉⲗⲉⲓ ⲛⲉⲡⲟⲩⲉⲓⲱⲧ⳿ ⲛⲁϫⲡⲟⲟⲩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲩⲙⲁⲁⲩ ⲉⲩⲥⲃ︦ⲃⲏⲩ ⲁⲗⲗⲁ ⲡⲥⲃ︦ⲃⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲉ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲛ︤ⲁ︥ ⲁϥϭⲛ̄ϩⲏⲩ ⲧⲏⲣϥ

i18n.en: His disciples said to him: Is circumcision useful or not? He said to them: If it were useful, their father would beget them from their mother already circumcised. But the true circumcision in spirit has become profitable in every respect.

notes.official: Greek ⲱⲫⲉⲗⲉⲓ is 'useful' and native ϭⲛ̄ϩⲏⲩ is 'profitable', so the English shows the change of word. 'The true circumcision in spirit' compares with Rom 2:29. 'Spirit' is lower case under the pneuma entry; English versions of Romans also differ on the capital. 'Their father' is a human father and is lower case. ⟨ⲙ̄⟩ⲙⲟⲛ has a supplied letter rendered silently. The central `brit-milah-circumcision-covenant` entry (Hebrew, Gen 17) is not cited (see `logion-53-circumcision-in-spirit-thomas-woh`).

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉϩⲛ̄ⲙⲁⲕⲁⲣⲓⲟⲥ ⲛⲉ ⲛϩⲏⲕⲉ ϫⲉⲧⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲧⲉ ⲧⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ ⲛⲙ̄ⲡⲏⲩⲉ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of the heavens.

notes.official: Thomas combines the two synoptic forms. It has plain 'the poor' and 'yours' as in Lk 6:20, and 'the kingdom of the heavens' as in Mt 5:3. Matthew has 'the poor in spirit' and 'theirs'; Luke has 'the kingdom of God'. The English keeps the person shift and the plural 'heavens' (central `kingdom-of-heaven-basileia-tōn-ouranōn-mt-distinctive-cross-corpus-hebrew-malkhut-shamayim`). As a synoptic-parallel beatitude, the saying cites the central beatitudes entry. 'Poor' pairs with 'poverty' at logion 3.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲡⲉⲧⲁⲙⲉⲥⲧⲉⲡⲉϥ⳿ⲉⲓⲱⲧ⳿ ⲁⲛ⳿ ⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉϥⲙⲁⲁⲩ ϥⲛⲁϣⲣ̄ⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ⲁⲛ ⲛⲁⲉⲓ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲛ̄ϥⲙⲉⲥⲧⲉⲛⲉϥ̂ⲥⲛⲏⲩ · ⲙⲛ̄ⲛⲉϥⲥⲱⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ϥϥⲉⲓ ⲙⲡⲉϥⲥⳁⲟⲥ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁϩⲉ ϥⲛⲁϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲁⲛ ⲉϥⲟ ⲛ̄ⲁⲝⲓⲟⲥ ⲛⲁⲉⲓ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Whoever does not hate his father and his mother will not be able to become a disciple to me. And whoever does not hate his brothers and his sisters and take up his cross as I do will not be worthy of me.

notes.official:
**The staurogram.** ⲙⲡⲉϥⲥⳁⲟⲥ writes σταυρός with the tau-rho ligature (staurogram), the only one in Block B. It is expanded silently to 'cross' under the extended nomina-sacra convention; on the staurogram as an early Christian scribal device see Hurtado, The Earliest Christian Artifacts (2006). In the source the ligature is encoded as U+2CC1 COPTIC SMALL LETTER SAMPI rather than U+2CE8 COPTIC SYMBOL TAU RO, a look-alike substitution recorded for the data maintainers.

Compare Lk 14:26-27 and Mt 10:37-38, and the doublet at logion 101. ⲛ̄ⲧⲁϩⲉ 'in my manner' is 'as I do'. 'His father' is lower case.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲡⲉⲧⲁϩⲥⲟⲩⲱⲛⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ ⲁϥ⳿ϩⲉ ⲉⲩⲡⲧⲱⲙⲁ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲉⲛⲧⲁϩϩⲉⲉ ⲁⲡⲧⲱⲙⲁ ⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ ⲙ̄ⲡϣⲁ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟϥ ⲁⲛ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Whoever has come to know the world has found a corpse; and whoever has found a corpse, the world is not worthy of him.

notes.official: 'Corpse' renders ⲡⲧⲱⲙⲁ here and twice at 60. The doublet at logion 80 has ⲥⲱⲙⲁ 'body' instead, and the two words are kept apart so that the variation stays visible (see `ptoma-corpse-thomas-woh`). 'Is not worthy of him' renders ⲙ̄ⲡϣⲁ, the same English as ⲁⲝⲓⲟⲥ at 55.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲧⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲓⲱⲧ ⲉⲥⲧ⟨ⲛ̄⟩ⲧⲱ(ⲛ) ⲁⲩⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲉⲩⲛ̄ⲧⲁϥ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ ⲛ̄ⲛⲟⲩϭⲣⲟϭ ⲉ̣ⲛ̣[ⲁⲛⲟ]ⲩϥ⳿ ⲁⲡⲉϥϫⲁϫⲉ ⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲩϣⲏ⳿ ⲁϥⲥⲓⲧⲉ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲍⲓⲍ̣ⲁ̣ⲛ̣ⲓ̣[ⲟ]ⲛ̣ ̣ⲉ̣ϫ̣ⲛⲡⲉϭⲣ̣ⲟ̣[ϭ ⲉ]ⲧⲛⲁⲛⲟⲩϥ⳿ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲕⲟⲟⲩ ⲉϩⲱⲗⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲍⲓⲍⲁⲛⲓⲟⲛ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁⲩ ϫⲉⲙⲏⲡⲱⲥ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲃⲱⲕ ϫⲉⲉⲛⲁϩⲱⲗⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲍⲓⲍⲁⲛⲓⲟⲛ ⲛⲧⲉⲧⲛϩⲱⲗⲉ                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      ⲙ̄ⲡⲥⲟⲩⲟ ⲛⲙ̄ⲙⲁϥ̂ ϩⲙ̄ⲫⲟⲟⲩ ⲅⲁⲣ ⲙ̄ⲡⲱϩ︤ⲥ︥ ⲛ̄ⲍⲓⲍⲁⲛⲓⲟⲛ ⲛⲁⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ⳿ ⲥⲉϩⲟⲗⲟⲩ ⲛ̄ⲥⲉⲣⲟⲕϩⲟⲩ

i18n.en: Jesus said: The kingdom of the Father is like a man who had [good] seed. His enemy came by night and sowed [darnel] upon the [good seed]. The man did not let them pull up the darnel. He said to them: Lest you go in order to pull up the darnel, and pull up the wheat along with it. For on the day of the harvest the darnel will appear; they will be pulled up and burned.

notes.official:
**Restorations.** '[good] seed', '[darnel]' and 'the [good seed]' stand on partly restored tokens. Letters marked with an underdot in the source are uncertain but not restored, and they are not bracketed. ⲉⲥⲧ⟨ⲛ̄⟩ⲧⲱ(ⲛ) has supplied letters, rendered silently.

**Thomas's form of the parable.** Compare Mt 13:24-30. Thomas omits the slaves' question, so 'them' in 'did not let them pull up' has no antecedent in the saying. 'Darnel' matches matthew-woh (see `logion-57-darnel-parable-vocabulary-thomas-woh`). ϫⲉⲉⲛⲁϩⲱⲗⲉ is literally 'saying, "We will pull up"' (Dilley: optative/second future), a quoted intention rendered 'in order to pull up'. Dilley notes that the conjunctive ⲛ̄ⲥⲉ may be restored in the last clause; the sense is unchanged.

**Source note.** The `text` field contains a run of 454 spaces between ⲛⲧⲉⲧⲛϩⲱⲗⲉ and ⲙ̄ⲡⲥⲟⲩⲟ, an export artefact. The normalised layer runs on without a gap, and nothing is missing.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲟⲩⲙⲁⲕⲁⲣⲓⲟⲥ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁϩϩⲓⲥⲉ ⲁϥϩⲉ ⲁⲡⲱⲛϩ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Blessed is the man who has suffered; he has found life.

notes.official: ϩⲓⲥⲉ covers 'toil, labour' and 'suffer'. 'Who has suffered' follows the beatitude form; compare Jas 1:12 and 1 Pet 3:14 (see `hise-suffer-toil-thomas-woh`). The singular formula is 'Blessed is'.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉϭⲱϣⲧ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁⲡⲉⲧⲟⲛϩ ϩⲱⲥ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲟⲛϩ ϩⲓⲛⲁ ϫⲉⲛⲉⲧⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲩ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲓⲛⲉ ⲉⲛⲁⲩ ⲉⲣⲟϥ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁϣϭⲙ̄ϭⲟⲙ ⲁⲛ ⲉⲛⲁⲩ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Look to the living one while you are alive, so that you do not die and seek to see him and be unable to see.

notes.official:
**The negative.** The diplomatic ϩⲓⲛⲁ ϫⲉⲛⲉⲧⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲩ writes the negative optative with a single ⲛ (ⲛⲉ- for ⲛ̄ⲛⲉ-, as at THOM-21 and 22); the normalised layer reads ⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲙⲟⲩ, and the English reads it as a negative ('so that you do not die').

ϭⲱϣⲧ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁ- is 'look to', keeping the visual verb that the rest of the saying develops (see `goosht-look-watch-thomas-woh`). 'The living one' is lower case.

paragraphs.text: ⟨ⲁⲩⲛⲁⲩ⟩ ⲁⲩⲥⲁⲙⲁⲣⲉⲓⲧⲏⲥ ⲉϥϥⲓ ⲛ̄ⲛⲟⲩϩⲓⲉⲓⲃ · ⲉϥⲃⲏⲕ̂ ⲉϩⲟⲩⲛ ⲉϯⲟⲩⲇⲁⲓⲁ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ̂ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉϥ̂ⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ϫⲉⲡⲏ̣ ⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲱⲧⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉϩⲓⲉⲓⲃ̂ ⲡⲉϫⲁⲩ ⲛⲁϥ ϫⲉ̣ⲕⲁⲁⲥ ⲉϥⲛⲁⲙⲟⲟⲩⲧϥ · ⲛ̄ϥⲟⲩⲟⲙϥ⳿ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁⲩ ϩⲱⲥ ⲉϥⲟⲛϩ ϥⲛⲁⲟⲩⲟⲙϥ̂ ⲁⲛ ⲁⲗⲗⲁ ⲉϥϣⲁⲙⲟⲟⲩⲧϥ⳿ ⲛ̄ϥϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲡⲧⲱⲙⲁ ⲡⲉϫⲁⲩ ϫⲉⲛ̄ⲕⲉⲥⲙⲟⲧ⳿ ϥⲛⲁϣⲁⲥ ⲁⲛ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁⲩ ϫⲉⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲧⲛ̄ ϩⲱⲧ̂ⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄ ϣⲓⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁⲟⲩⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ ⲛⲏⲧⲛ̄ ⲉϩⲟⲩⲛ ⲉⲩⲁⲛⲁⲡⲁⲩⲥⲓⲥ ϫⲉⲕⲁⲁⲥ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲧⲛ̄ϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲧⲱⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ⲥⲉⲟⲩⲱⲙ⳿ⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄

i18n.en: ⟨They saw⟩ a Samaritan carrying a lamb, going into Judea. He said to his disciples: That one is around the lamb. They said to him: So that he may kill it and eat it. He said to them: While it is alive he will not eat it, but only if he kills it and it becomes a corpse. They said: Otherwise he will not be able to do it. He said to them: You too, seek a place for yourselves within repose, so that you do not become a corpse and be eaten.

notes.official:
**'⟨They saw⟩'.** The manuscript begins ⲁⲩⲥⲁⲙⲁⲣⲉⲓⲧⲏⲥ 'a Samaritan' (with Lycopolitan ⲁ- for the preposition ⲉ-) and has no main verb. Dilley supplies the whole verb ⟨ⲁⲩⲛⲁⲩ⟩ 'they saw', and Lambdin prints '<They saw>'. A silent rendering would tell the reader that the manuscript contains the verb. The English therefore marks it with English angle brackets, which are used here for the first time in Thomas (see `whole-word-supply-angle-brackets-convention-thomas-woh`).

**The crux.** ϫⲉⲡⲏ̣ ⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲱⲧⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉϩⲓⲉⲓⲃ is literally 'That one is around the lamb'. Translations often supply words, for example '(Why does) that man (carry) the lamb around?'. The manuscript reading stands in the line (see `logion-60-samaritan-crux-thomas-woh`). 'Corpse' links the saying to logion 56, and 'a place … within repose' uses τόπος and ἀνάπαυσις (see `ptoma-corpse-thomas-woh` and `kim-anapausis-mton-movement-repose-rest-thomas-woh`).

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲟⲩⲛ̄ⲥⲛⲁⲩ ⲛⲁⲙ̄ⲧⲟⲛ⳿ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ ϩⲓⲟⲩϭⲗⲟϭ ⲡⲟⲩⲁ ⲛⲁⲙⲟⲩ ⲡⲟⲩⲁ ⲛⲁⲱⲛϩ ⲡⲉϫⲉⲥⲁⲗⲱⲙⲏ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲕ⳿ⲛⲓⲙ⳿ ⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ ϩⲱⲥ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲁ ⲁⲕⲧⲉⲗⲟ ⲉϫⲙ̄ⲡⲁϭⲗⲟϭ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁⲕ⳿ⲟⲩⲱⲙ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲧⲣⲁⲡⲉⲍⲁ ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ⲛⲁⲥ ϫⲉⲁⲛⲟⲕ⳿ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲉⲧϣⲟⲟⲡ⳿ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧ⳿ϣⲏϣ ⲁⲩϯ ⲛⲁⲉⲓ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ⲛⲁⲡⲁⲉⲓⲱⲧ⳿ ⲁⲛⲟⲕ⳿ⲧⲉⲕ⳿ⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ ⲉⲧⲃⲉⲡⲁⲉⲓ ϯϫⲱ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲥ ϫⲉϩⲟⲧⲁⲛ ⲉϥϣⲁϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲉϥϣⲏϥ⳿ ϥⲛⲁⲙⲟⲩϩ̣ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ ϩⲟⲧⲁⲛ ⲇⲉ ⲉϥϣⲁⲛϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲉϥⲡⲏϣ ϥⲛⲁⲙⲟⲩϩ ⲛ̄ⲕⲁⲕⲉ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Two will rest on a bed: one will die, one will live. Salome said: Who are you, man? As though from someone, you have climbed onto my bed and eaten from my table. Jesus said to her: I am the one who exists from the one who is equal. I was given from the things of my Father. ⟨Salome said:⟩ I am your disciple. Because of this I say: When he is destroyed, he will be filled with light; but when he is divided, he will be filled with darkness.

notes.official:
**Salome.** A Salome is among the women at the cross and the tomb in Mk 15:40 and 16:1, and Salome questions Jesus in the Gospel of the Egyptians quoted by Clement (Stromata 3). Thomas does not identify her further (see `salome-name-thomas-woh`). 'I am your disciple' has no speech formula. The feminine possessive ⲧⲉⲕ- shows that the speaker is Salome. English cannot mark this, and under the register convention the English supplies no formula; the question is escalated for review.

**'As though from someone'.** ϩⲱⲥ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲁ takes ⲟⲩⲁ as the indefinite 'someone': Salome treats Jesus as a stranger who has taken a guest's place on her couch. 'From the One' would read a title into the indefinite pronoun. The opening line compares with Lk 17:34, and 'I was given from the things of my Father' compares with Mt 11:27.

**'The one who is equal' and the crux.** ⲡⲉⲧϣⲏϣ is the stative of ϣⲱϣ 'be equal'; Lambdin renders 'the undivided'. In the last sentence the manuscript has ⲉϥϣⲏϥ 'destroyed, desolate'. Dilley notes that the passage may be corrupt and records the uncertain emendation ϣⲏϣ 'equal' (Layton 1989, p. 74), which would answer ⲡⲉⲧϣⲏϣ above and contrast with ⲡⲏϣ 'divided'. The manuscript reading stands in the line (see `shesh-equal-and-logion-61-crux-thomas-woh`). Native ⲙ̄ⲧⲟⲛ is 'rest'.

**'Two will rest on a bed'.** ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ here is not the adverb 'there': ⲙ̄ⲧⲟⲛ is reflexive (ⲙ̄ⲧⲟⲛ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟ=), and the corpus normalises the form as ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲩ, the object pronoun (corrected at sign-off).

**⟨Salome said:⟩.** The Coptic has no speech formula before 'I am your disciple', but the feminine possessive ⲧⲉⲕ- marks Salome as the speaker; without the formula an English reader would take the words as Jesus'. The formula is supplied in angle brackets, the sign for English words with no source wording, as a narrow exception ratified at sign-off (2026-11-01).

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫ̣ⲉ̣ⲓ̣︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲉⲓ̈ϫⲱ ⲛ̄ⲛⲁⲙⲩⲥⲧⲏⲣⲓⲟⲛ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉ̣[ⲧⲙⲡϣⲁ] ⲛ̣[ⲛⲁ]ⲙ̣ⲩⲥⲧⲏⲣⲓⲟⲛ̣ ⲡ̣ⲉ̣[ⲧ]ⲉ̣̣ⲧ̣ⲉ̣ⲕ̣⳿ⲟⲩⲛⲁⲙ ⲛⲁⲁϥ ⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲣⲉⲧⲉⲕϩⲃⲟⲩⲣ̂ ⲉⲓⲙⲉ ϫⲉⲉⲥⲣⲟⲩ

i18n.en: Jesus said: It is to [those who are worthy] of [my] mysteries that I tell my mysteries. [What] your right hand does, do not let your left hand know what it is doing.

notes.official: **Restoration and word order.** ⲛ̄ⲛⲉ̣[ⲧⲙⲡϣⲁ], ⲛ̣[ⲛⲁ]ⲙⲩⲥⲧⲏⲣⲓⲟⲛ and ⲡ̣ⲉ̣[ⲧ]ⲉ… are partly restored, hence '[those who are worthy]', '[my]' and '[What]'. The corpus parses ⲉⲓ̈ϫⲱ as a focalising present, which puts the emphasis on the recipients. The draft's 'I tell my mysteries to …' is changed to the cleft 'It is to … that I tell my mysteries' (see `mysterion-mysteries-thomas-woh`). 'Mysteries' is the word of Mk 4:11. The second sentence compares with Mt 6:3. The diplomatic ⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲣⲉ is normalised to the negative jussive ⲙⲡⲣ̄ⲧⲣⲉ 'do not let'.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲛⲉⲩⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲗⲟⲩⲥⲓⲟⲥ ⲉⲩⲛ̄ⲧⲁϥ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ ⲛ̄ϩⲁϩ ⲛ̄ⲭⲣⲏⲙⲁ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ϫⲉϯⲛⲁⲣ̄ⲭⲣⲱ ⲛ̄ⲛⲁⲭⲣⲏⲙⲁ ϫⲉⲕⲁⲁⲥ ⲉⲉⲓⲛⲁϫⲟ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲱ[[ϩ]]ⲥϩ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲧⲱϭⲉ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲙⲟⲩϩ ⲛ̄ⲛⲁⲉϩⲱⲣ ⲛ̄ⲕⲁⲣⲡⲟⲥ ϣⲓⲛⲁ ϫⲉⲛⲓⲣ̄ϭⲣⲱϩ ⲗ̄ⲗⲁⲁⲩ ⲛⲁⲉⲓ ⲛⲉ ⲛⲉϥⲙⲉⲉⲩⲉ ⲉⲣⲟⲟⲩ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲉϥϩⲏⲧ⳿ ⲁⲩⲱ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲩϣⲏ ⲉⲧⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ ⲁϥⲙⲟⲩ ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲩⲙ̄ⲙⲁϫⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟϥ⳿ ⲙⲁⲣⲉϥ⳿ⲥⲱⲧⲙ

i18n.en: Jesus said: There was a rich man who had much money. He said: I will use my money to sow and reap and plant and fill my storehouses with fruit, so that I lack nothing. These were the things he was thinking in his heart, and that night he died. Whoever has ears, let him hear.

notes.official:
Compare Lk 12:16-21. The closing formula is the short one ('Whoever has ears, let him hear'), without the 'to hear' of logia 8 and 21.

**Source note.** ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲱ[[ϩ]]ⲥϩ shows a letter erased by the scribe (Dilley: rasura) and a metathesis. The normalised layer reads ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲱϩⲥ 'and reap'. The double square brackets mark a scribal erasure, not a modern restoration, so no English word is bracketed.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲟⲩⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲛⲉⲩⲛ̄ⲧⲁϥ̣ ϩⲛ̄ϣⲙ̄ⲙⲟ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲣⲉϥⲥⲟⲃⲧⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲇⲓⲡⲛⲟⲛ ⲁϥϫⲟⲟⲩ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉϥϩⲙϩ︤ⲁ︥︤ⲗ︥ ϣⲓⲛⲁ ⲉϥⲛⲁⲧⲱϩⲙ ⲛ̄ⲛ̄ϣⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲉⲓ ⲁϥⲃⲱⲕ⳿ ⲙ̄ⲡϣⲟⲣⲡ⳿ · ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁϥ⳿ ϫⲉⲡⲁϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ ⲧⲱϩⲙ̄ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲕ⳿ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ϫⲉⲟⲩⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲉⲓ ϩⲛ̄ϩⲟⲙⲧ⳿ ⲁϩⲉⲛⲉⲙⲡⲟⲣⲟⲥ ⲥⲉⲛ̄ⲛⲏⲩ ϣⲁⲣⲟⲉⲓ ⲉⲣⲟⲩϩⲉ ϯⲛⲁⲃⲱⲕ⳿ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲟⲩⲉϩⲥⲁϩⲛⲉ ⲛⲁⲩ ϯⲣ̄ⲡⲁⲣⲁⲓⲧⲉⲓ ⲙ̄ⲡⲇⲓⲡⲛⲟⲛ ⲁϥⲃⲱⲕ⳿ ϣⲁⲕⲉⲟⲩⲁ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁϥ⳿ ϫⲉⲁⲡⲁϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ ⲧⲱϩⲙ̄ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲕ⳿ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁϥ ϫⲉⲁⲉⲓⲧⲟⲟⲩⲟⲩⲏⲉⲓ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲥⲉⲣ̄ⲁⲓⲧⲉⲓ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩϩⲏⲙⲉⲣⲁ ϯⲛⲁⲥⲣ̄ϥⲉ ⲁ(ⲛ) ⲁϥⲉⲓ ϣⲁⲕⲉⲟⲩⲁ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁϥ⳿ ϫⲉⲡⲁϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ ⲧⲱϩⲙ̄ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲕ⳿ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁϥ ϫⲉⲡⲁϣⲃⲏⲣ⳿ ⲛⲁⲣ̄ϣⲉⲗⲉⲉⲧ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁⲛⲟⲕ⳿ ⲉⲧⲛⲁⲣ̄ⲇⲓⲡⲛⲟⲛ ϯⲛⲁϣⲓ ⲁⲛ ϯⲣ̄ⲡⲁⲣⲁⲓⲧⲉⲓ ⲙ̄ⲡⲇⲓⲡⲛⲟⲛ⳿ ⲁϥ⳿ⲃⲱⲕ⳿ ϣⲁⲕⲉⲟⲩⲁ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁϥ ϫⲉⲡⲁϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ ⲧⲱϩⲙ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲕ⳿ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲛⲁϥ⳿ ϫⲉⲁⲉⲓⲧⲟⲟⲩ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲕⲱⲙⲏ ⲉⲉⲓⲃⲏⲕ⳿ ⲁϫⲓⲛ̄ϣⲱⲙ ϯⲛⲁϣⲓ ⲁⲛ ϯⲣ̄ⲡⲁⲣⲁⲓⲧⲉⲓ ⲁϥⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲡϩⲙϩ︤ⲁ︥︤ⲗ︥ ⲁϥϫⲟⲟⲥ ⲁⲡⲉϥϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ ϫⲉⲛⲉⲛⲧⲁⲕ⳿ⲧⲁϩⲙⲟⲩ ⲁⲡⲇⲓⲡⲛⲟⲛ ⲁⲩⲡⲁⲣⲁⲓⲧⲉⲓ ⲡⲉϫⲉⲡϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉϥϩⲙϩⲁ︤ⲗ︥ ϫⲉⲃⲱⲕ⳿ ⲉⲡⲥⲁ ⲛⲃⲟⲗ ⲁⲛϩⲓⲟⲟⲩⲉ ⲛⲉⲧⲕⲛⲁϩⲉ ⲉⲣⲟⲟⲩ ⲉⲛⲓⲟⲩ ϫⲉⲕⲁⲁⲥ ⲉⲩⲛⲁ̣ⲣ̣̄ⲇ̣ⲓ̣ⲡ̣ⲛⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ⲣⲉϥⲧⲟⲟⲩ ⲙⲛ̄ⲛⲉϣⲟⲧ̣[ⲉ ⲥⲉⲛⲁⲃ]ⲱ̣ⲕ̣ ⲁⲛ⳿ ⲉϩⲟⲩⲛ⳿ ⲉⲛⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ ⲙⲡⲁⲓ̈ⲱⲧ⳿

i18n.en: Jesus said: A man had guests. And when he had prepared the dinner, he sent his slave to invite the guests. He went to the first; he said to him: My master invites you. He said: I have money due from some merchants; they are coming to me in the evening; I will go and give them instructions. I ask to be excused from the dinner. He went to another; he said to him: My master has invited you. He said to him: I have bought a house, and they are asking me for a day; I will not have time. He came to another; he said to him: My master invites you. He said to him: My friend is going to be married, and I am the one who is to hold the dinner; I will not be able to come. I ask to be excused from the dinner. He went to another; he said to him: My master invites you. He said to him: I have bought a village; I am going to collect the rents; I will not be able to come. I ask to be excused. The slave came; he said to his master: Those whom you invited to the dinner have asked to be excused. The master said to his slave: Go outside to the roads; those whom you find, bring them, so that they may dine. Buyers and [merchants will] not [enter] the places of my Father.

notes.official:
**Vocabulary.** ϣⲙ̄ⲙⲟ 'stranger' is 'guests', since these are the invited. ⲕⲱⲙⲏ is 'village', as at logion 31. 'Money due from some merchants' renders 'money against some merchants' (see `logion-64-dinner-parable-vocabulary-thomas-woh`). ϩⲙϩⲁⲗ is 'slave' and ϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ 'master'. ⲣ̄ϣⲉⲗⲉⲉⲧ 'be married' shares its root with the 'bridal chamber' of 75. Compare Lk 14:16-24 and Mt 22:1-10; Thomas's excuses are commercial.

**The closing line.** ⲛ̄ⲣⲉϥⲧⲟⲟⲩ ⲙⲛ̄ⲛⲉϣⲟⲧ̣[ⲉ ⲥⲉⲛⲁⲃ]ⲱ̣ⲕ̣ ⲁⲛ is partly restored, hence 'Buyers and [merchants will] not [enter]'. The plural 'the places of my Father' is kept. Greek ⲉⲙⲡⲟⲣⲟⲥ and native ⲉϣⲟⲧⲉ are both 'merchants'. Whether the master of the parable or Jesus speaks the closing line is left open, as in the Coptic. ⲁ(ⲛ) has a supplied letter, rendered silently.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ϫⲉⲟⲩⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲛⲭⲣ̣ⲏ̣[ⲥⲧⲟ]ⲥ̣ ⲛⲉⲩⲛ[ⲧⲁϥ] ⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ⲉⲗⲟⲟⲗⲉ ⲁϥⲧⲁ⳿ⲁϥ ⲛ̄ϩ̣ⲛⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲉ ϣⲓⲛⲁ ⲉⲩⲛⲁⲣ̄ϩⲱⲃ⳿ ⲉⲣⲟϥ⳿ ⲛ̄ϥϫⲓ ⲙ̣̄ⲡⲉϥⲕⲁⲣ⳿ⲡⲟⲥ ⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲟⲧⲟⲩ ⲁϥϫⲟⲟⲩ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉϥϩⲙϩ︤ⲁ︥︤ⲗ︥ ϫⲉⲕⲁⲁⲥ ⲉⲛⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲉ ⲛⲁϯ ⲛⲁϥ⳿ ⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲁⲣⲡⲟⲥ ⲙ̄ⲡⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ⲉⲗⲟⲟⲗⲉ ⲁⲩⲉⲙⲁϩⲧⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉϥϩⲙ̄ϩ︤ⲁ︥︤ⲗ︥ ⲁⲩϩⲓⲟⲩⲉ ⲉⲣⲟϥ⳿ ⲛⲉⲕⲉⲕⲟⲩⲉⲓ ⲡⲉ ⲛ̄ⲥⲉ⳿ⲙⲟⲟⲩⲧϥ⳿ ⲁⲡϩⲙϩ︤ⲁ︥︤ⲗ︥ ⲃⲱⲕ⳿ ⲁϥϫⲟⲟⲥ ⲉⲡⲉϥϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ ⲡⲉϫⲉⲡⲉϥϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ ϫⲉⲙⲉϣⲁⲕ⳿ ⲙ̣̄ⲡⲉϥ⳿ⲥⲟⲩⲱⲛⲟⲩ ⲁϥϫⲟⲟⲩ ⲛ̄ⲕⲉϩⲙϩ︤ⲁ︥︤ⲗ︥ ⲁⲛⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲉ ϩⲓⲟⲩⲉ ⲉⲡⲕⲉⲟⲩⲁ ⲧⲟⲧⲉ ⲁⲡϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ ϫⲟⲟⲩ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉϥϣⲏⲣⲉ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ⳿ ϫⲉⲙⲉϣⲁⲕ⳿ ⲥⲉⲛⲁϣⲓⲡⲉ ϩⲏⲧϥ⳿ ⲙ̄ⲡⲁϣⲏⲣⲉ ⲁⲛ⳿ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲉ ⲉⲧⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ ⲉⲡⲉⲓⲥⲉⲥⲟⲟⲩⲛ ϫⲉⲛ̄ⲧⲟϥ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲉⲕⲗⲏⲣⲟⲛⲟⲙⲟⲥ ⲙ̄ⲡⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ⲉⲗⲟⲟⲗⲉ ⲁⲩϭⲟⲡϥ⳿ ⲁⲩⲙⲟⲟⲩⲧϥ⳿ ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲩⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲁϫⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟϥ̂ ⲙⲁⲣⲉϥⲥⲱⲧⲙ̄

i18n.en: He said: A [good] man [had] a vineyard. He gave it to farmers so that they would work it and he would receive its fruit from them. He sent his slave so that the farmers would give him the fruit of the vineyard. They seized his slave and beat him; a little more and they would have killed him. The slave went and told his master. His master said: Perhaps he did not know them. He sent another slave; the farmers beat the other one. Then the master sent his son. He said: Perhaps they will feel shame before my son. Those farmers, since they knew that he was the heir of the vineyard, seized him and killed him. Whoever has ears, let him hear.

notes.official:
**The restoration.** The source restores ⲭⲣⲏ[ⲥⲧⲟ]ⲥ 'good' (χρηστός, an adjective Thomas uses again at logion 90). It is printed '[good]'. An alternative restoration, ⲭⲣⲏ[ⲥⲧⲏ]ⲥ 'creditor, usurer' (χρήστης), has been proposed and would make the owner a moneylender. '[had]' stands on the partly restored ⲛⲉⲩⲛ[ⲧⲁϥ].

**The crux.** ⲙⲉϣⲁⲕ ⲙ̣̄ⲡⲉϥⲥⲟⲩⲱⲛⲟⲩ as written means 'Perhaps he did not know them' (the slave did not recognise the farmers). Dilley records the uncertain emendation ⲙ̣̄ⲡⲟⲩ- 'perhaps they did not know him' (Layton 1989, p. 78), which is widely printed. The manuscript reading stands in the line (see `logion-65-vineyard-restoration-and-crux-thomas-woh`). ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲉ is 'farmers' and ϣⲓⲡⲉ ϩⲏⲧ= is 'feel shame before', where Mk 12:6 has 'respect'. Compare Mk 12:1-9. Thomas has no allusion to Isa 5, no killing of the slaves and no punishment of the farmers.

**Source note.** The lemma aid counts four supplied spans, while `text` shows two bracket groups; the normalised layer also supplies ⲉⲣⲉ- in ϫⲉⲕⲁⲁⲥ ⲉ(ⲣⲉ)ⲛⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲉ.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲙⲁⲧⲥⲉⲃⲟⲉⲓ ⲉⲡⲱⲛⲉ ⲡⲁⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲩⲥⲧⲟϥ̂ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ⳿ ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲛⲉⲧ⳿ⲕⲱⲧ⳿ ⲛ̄ⲧⲟϥ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲱⲱⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ⲕⲱϩ

i18n.en: Jesus said: Show me the stone that the builders rejected: that one is the cornerstone.

notes.official: Compare Ps 118:22 and Mk 12:10-11, where the stone saying likewise follows the parable of the vineyard. ⲙⲁⲧⲥⲉⲃⲟⲉⲓ is 'Show me', ⲧⲥⲁⲃⲟ in the sense 'make known' as at logion 24.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲡⲉⲧⲥⲟⲟⲩⲛ ⲙ̄ⲡⲧⲏⲣϥ⳿ ⲉϥⲣ̄ϭⲣⲱϩ ⲟⲩⲁⲁϥ ⟨ϥ⟩ⲣ̄ϭⲣⲱϩ ⲙ̄ⲡⲙⲁ ⲧⲏⲣϥ⳿

i18n.en: Jesus said: Whoever knows the All but is lacking in himself is lacking entirely.

notes.official: **Parse.** ⲉϥⲣ̄ϭⲣⲱϩ ⲟⲩⲁⲁϥ is read 'is lacking in himself', and ⲙ̄ⲡⲙⲁ ⲧⲏⲣϥ (literally 'the whole place') as the adverbial 'entirely'. Other parses take ⲟⲩⲁⲁϥ with 'the All', or keep 'the whole place'. The choice is marked `inferred` (see `logion-67-lacking-entirely-thomas-woh`). ⲙⲁ is idiomatic here, so the topos/ma entry is not applied. The edition supplies ⟨ϥ⟩ before the second ⲣ̄ϭⲣⲱϩ, rendered silently. 'The All' follows logion 2.

paragraphs.text: ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉⲛⲧⲱⲧⲛ ϩⲙⲙⲁⲕⲁⲣⲓⲟⲥ ϩⲟⲧⲁⲛ ⲉⲩϣⲁⲛⲙⲉⲥⲧⲉⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄ ⲛ̄ⲥⲉⲣ̄ⲇⲓⲱⲕⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲥⲉⲛⲁϩⲉ ⲁⲛ ⲉⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲙⲁ ⲉⲛⲧⲁⲩⲇⲓⲱⲕⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲱⲧⲛ̄ ϩⲣⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧϥ̅

i18n.en: Jesus said: Blessed are you whenever they hate you and persecute you; and they will not find a place in the place where they have persecuted you.

notes.official:
Compare Mt 5:11 and Lk 6:22. The second clause, literally 'and they will not find a place in the place where they have persecuted you', is obscure. The English keeps it literally, with both 'place' words (τόπος and ⲙⲁ) (see `logia-68-69-persecution-beatitudes-wording-thomas-woh`).
